items.title: altero documentation
items.text:
altero lets you synchronize Zotero libraries on a server you control. Use Zotero Desktop, the browser interface, or both.

Warning

Keep a current backup of important libraries and don’t rely on altero as your only copy yet.

items.title: For contributors
items.text:
Start with the development guide. Use the compatibility reference and database schema when changing server behavior. For browser work, see the design system and implementation notes.

To help test, follow two-client testing, desktop compatibility checks, or the Podman procedure. These pages include the scope and limits of recorded results.

items.title: Terms used in these guides
items.text:
• Instance: one altero installation, including its database and attachment storage.
  • Library: a personal or group Zotero library.
  • API key: a credential used by Zotero Desktop to synchronize. Signing into the browser does not replace it.
  • Connected application: software you have approved to access your account with limited, expiring tokens.
  • Instance administrator: someone who manages the server and accounts. This role does not automatically grant access to other people's library contents.

items.title: Administration
items.text:
This page covers operations that affect the altero instance, accounts, groups or complete libraries.

For your own password, sign-in methods and preferences, use Accounts and personal settings.

items.title: What an instance administrator can do
items.text:
Most altero permissions belong to a library. The instance administrator role is different: it can operate the server itself.

An instance administrator can manage accounts, retention, identity providers, registered applications and storage information. The role does not grant automatic access to other users' library contents. An administrator can count and operate libraries without being allowed to read their items, notes or files.

The first account that claims a fresh instance becomes an administrator. The last administrator cannot demote, suspend or delete themselves, so a working instance cannot be left without one through normal administration.

From the shell:

uv run altero user admin <username>
uv run altero user admin <username> --revoke

items.title: Common command-line tasks
items.text: The browser covers most routine administration. The command line remains useful for initial setup and recovery.

items.title: Accounts and credentials
items.text:
uv run altero user add <username> [--display-name NAME] [--id N]
uv run altero user list
uv run altero user password <username>
uv run altero user admin <username> [--revoke]
uv run altero user disable <username> [--undo]
uv run altero user revoke <username>
uv run altero user delete <username> [--yes]

uv run altero key add <username> [--name LABEL] [--read-only] [--groups]
uv run altero key list
uv run altero key revoke <key>

uv run altero oauth add <client-id> --redirect-uri URL [--scope SCOPE] [--confidential]
uv run altero oauth list
uv run altero oauth disable <client-id>
uv run altero oauth rotate-key

items.title: Groups
items.text:
uv run altero group add <name> --owner <username> [--public]
uv run altero group member <group-id> <username> [--role admin]
uv run altero group members <group-id>
uv run altero group role <group-id> <username> <member|admin>
uv run altero group remove <group-id> <username>
uv run altero group delete <group-id> [--yes]

items.title: Libraries and retention
items.text:
uv run altero library list
uv run altero library set-version <user|group> <id> <version>
uv run altero library export <user|group> <id> <archive.zip>
uv run altero library import <archive.zip> [--replace]

uv run altero retention show
uv run altero retention run [--dry-run] [--trash DAYS]

items.title: Desktop login approval
items.text:
uv run altero login list
uv run altero login approve <token> <username> [--key KEY]

items.title: Administration screens
items.text: The browser shows Administration only to an account with the instance-administrator role.

items.title: Overview
items.text: The overview reports the altero version, Web API version, database dialect, attachment directory and Alembic revision. It also shows account, library and group counts.

items.title: Storage
items.text:
Storage reports both:

  • on disk — the physical bytes the instance stores; and
  • counted across libraries — the sum each library would account for separately.

The totals differ because altero stores the same attachment content once per digest even if several libraries reference it.

The screen also identifies:

  • unreferenced files; and
  • attachments whose expected bytes are missing.

An attachment can be missing its bytes because they were never here, because they were swept, or because the server removed a stored file that did not match what was uploaded. In each case the client offers the file again on its next sync.

Removing unreferenced files is an explicit administrator action, not a timed retention rule. Recent files are left alone because an upload can temporarily exist on disk before the database row that references it is committed. The same action removes files a write into the store never finished, under the same grace period.

items.title: Accounts
items.text: The Accounts screen can create an account, reset access, suspend it, revoke credentials or delete it.

items.title: Create an account
items.text:
An administrator can create an account with a username and password. The initial password is shown once and should be handed to the user securely; the user can then change it.

Browser registration is available only when one of these conditions applies:

  • this is the first account on a fresh instance;
  • ALTERO_OPEN_REGISTRATION enables registration; or
  • the email address has been invited to a group.

items.title: Password reset
items.text:
An administrator can either set a password or issue a single-use link that lets the account holder choose a new one.

The link is valid for 12 hours. If the account has a confirmed address and outgoing mail is configured, altero can email it. The administrator is also shown the link so an instance without mail can still recover an account.

Optional self-service password reset is controlled by ALTERO_PASSWORD_RESET and requires an SMTP relay and ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL.

items.title: Suspend an account
items.text:
Suspension blocks every form of access:

  • browser sessions;
  • API keys used by Zotero Desktop; and
  • OAuth access tokens held by connected applications.

No library data is deleted. Re-enabling the account restores access with the existing credentials unless those credentials were separately revoked.

items.title: Revoke credentials
items.text:
Credential revocation signs out browser sessions and invalidates API keys without disabling or deleting the account.

This is appropriate for a lost device or leaked credential. The user can continue using the account after creating or receiving new credentials.

It does not disconnect third-party applications: their grants survive it. The account holder disconnects one under Settings → Connected applications, and an operator can stop a whole application for everybody with altero oauth disable <client-id>. Suspending the account stops its tokens along with everything else.

items.title: Delete an account
items.text:
Deleting an account removes its personal library. It is refused while the account owns a group, because altero will not guess who should inherit that group.

Deletion is also refused for your own currently signed-in administrator account and where it would remove the last administrator.

items.title: Sign-in providers
items.text:
Administration → Sign-in providers configures OpenID Connect and SAML 2.0 for browser sign-in.

Directory sign-in creates a browser session. The v3 API accepts API keys and OAuth access tokens, never that session cookie. Zotero Desktop still gets its API key from Settings → API keys.

items.title: Before adding a provider
items.text:
Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL first. The administration screen shows the redirect/callback address that must be registered with the identity provider.

Provider creation, updates and sign-in refuse to proceed without this setting. OIDC callbacks, SAML assertion recipients and the SAML service-provider identity always use it; request host headers cannot supply a substitute.

A callback mismatch is rejected by the provider before altero can complete sign-in.

Live integration tests cover Keycloak and SimpleSAMLphp. Other provider recipes below are marked unverified. See the fixture scope for the flows actually checked.

items.title: OpenID Connect
items.text:
Store the client credentials and provider settings in the administration screen. Client secrets are write-only: the interface can replace a secret but does not display the existing value.

Copy the provider's exact issuer value from its discovery document, including any trailing slash. Issuers must match in configuration, discovery and ID tokens, as required by OpenID Connect Discovery.

items.title: SSO-only mode
items.text:
Set ALTERO_SSO_ONLY=true to require an OIDC or SAML provider for browser sign-in. ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL is required. Desktop API keys and connected applications continue working; this setting controls browser authentication.

Before enabling it:

  1. Configure and test an enabled provider, including fresh identity confirmation for sensitive actions.
  2. Connect existing accounts under Settings → Sign-in and security, or choose whether the provider may create accounts.
  3. Keep shell access for recovery, then enable the setting and restart.

Matching email addresses never links identities. With no working provider, users cannot sign in. Initial local registration is disabled too.

In this mode, local passwords, passkeys, registration, reset links, email changes and local second factors are unavailable. Manage second factors at the provider. Old local sessions must sign in through a provider; sensitive actions require fresh provider confirmation, valid for five minutes. After a provider round trip, reselect an archive or reenter form data if navigation cleared it.

The last enabled provider linked to an account cannot be removed. Existing local credentials are retained: to recover from provider failure, disable ALTERO_SSO_ONLY from the server shell, restart, and use account-recovery commands. This mode does not add continuous directory synchronization.

items.title: SAML 2.0
items.text:
A SAML provider requires:

  • the identity provider entity ID;
  • the sign-on URL; and
  • one or more signing certificates in PEM form.

Multiple certificates can be stored during signing-key rollover.

Register the screen's Callback address as the assertion consumer service (ACS), using HTTP-POST. For a provider whose short name is campus, this is <public_url>/web/auth/saml/campus/acs. The service provider entity ID is public_url without a trailing slash.

When linking an account or confirming identity, complete the return to altero in the same signed-in browser within two minutes. An expired handoff requires starting again. See the SAML session handoff for protocol details.

The SAML implementation is deliberately limited to:

  • SP-initiated sign-in;
  • signed, unencrypted assertions; and
  • local sign-out only, with no SAML Single Logout.

items.title: Account creation and deprovisioning
items.text:
Automatic account creation through a provider is off by default. Turning it on allows identities accepted by that provider to create local altero accounts.

A provider can also require a claim and value, such as an entitlement or group. On each sign-in, altero checks the requirement. If a previously linked user no longer has the required claim, the local account is suspended, which also stops existing Zotero API keys.

This check happens at sign-in time. It cannot detect a person who leaves the organization and never attempts to sign in again; administrators must handle that case through the Accounts screen or another operational process.

It also needs a token or assertion to check. If the directory refuses sign-in before returning one, altero cannot observe the missing claim and that attempt does not suspend existing local sessions or API credentials.

Removing a provider removes the account links to it, not the local accounts themselves.

items.title: Provider recipes
items.text:
Use these settings with your own HTTPS addresses and client credentials. The examples use https://library.example.org for ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL. Choose a Short name before registering the callback; it becomes part of that address.

Protocol Address to register at the provider OIDC https://library.example.org/web/auth/sso/<short-name>/callback SAML, HTTP-POST ACS https://library.example.org/web/auth/saml/<short-name>/acs SAML service provider entity ID https://library.example.org

For OIDC, create a confidential web client using authorization code and S256 PKCE, accepting client_secret_post at its token endpoint. Altero sends the secret in the form body. Set Scopes to profile email; openid is added automatically. The default claim names are preferred_username, name and email. Keep ID tokens unencrypted. Discovery and token endpoints must be reachable by the altero server, as well as the sign-in page by the browser.

Choose whether the provider may create accounts. With creation off, an existing user first connects the provider from Settings → Sign-in and security. Matching an email address never links accounts automatically. Required claim names a literal top-level claim or SAML attribute; Required value must match the string or one entry in its list exactly.

items.title: Keycloak
items.text:
Tested provider: OIDC and SAML integration tests cover Keycloak. See test scope for the exercised flows and limits.

For OIDC, create an openid-connect client in the chosen realm. Enable client authentication and the standard authorization-code flow, require S256, and register the exact callback. Copy the client ID and generated secret into altero. Set Issuer to https://<keycloak-host>/realms/<realm>. Keycloak client settings describe these controls.

To require a group, add a group-membership mapper to this client's scope, emitting groups in the ID token or UserInfo. With full paths disabled, set altero's requirement to groups and the group name, such as researchers.

For SAML, create a saml client whose ID is altero's entity ID. Register the ACS, force POST responses and persistent NameIDs, enable assertion signing with RSA-SHA256, and disable assertion encryption and required client signatures. Copy the IdP issuer, HTTP-Redirect sign-on endpoint and signing certificate from the realm's /protocol/saml/descriptor into altero. Map user attributes to preferred_username, name and email as needed. The fixture's realm settings show the tested mapper and protocol choices.

items.title: Microsoft Entra ID
items.text:
Unverified with altero. This recipe follows Microsoft's authorization-code flow and OIDC endpoints.

Register a single-tenant application in App registrations. Add a Web redirect URI with altero's exact OIDC callback, and create a client secret. Enter the application/client ID and the secret's value, not its identifier, in altero. Use https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0 as Issuer, with the actual tenant UUID. The common and organizations endpoints do not provide the fixed issuer this configuration requires. Use authorization code; implicit/hybrid ID-token delivery is not needed.

For an entitlement, define an app role with a value such as altero, assign test users to it, and set Required claim to roles and Required value to altero. The role must appear in the ID token. Altero does not resolve group-overage links through Microsoft Graph.

items.title: Okta
items.text:
Unverified with altero. Follow Okta's web application registration. Choose OIDC and Web Application, enable authorization code, register the exact callback, and assign the intended users or groups to the application.

Configure the client's token_endpoint_auth_method as client_secret_post using Okta's client settings/API; its default is client_secret_basic, while altero sends form credentials. See client authentication. Enter the client ID and secret in altero.

Use the org issuer https://<your-okta-domain> for ordinary sign-in. If using a custom authorization server, copy its exact issuer, such as https://<your-okta-domain>/oauth2/<authorization-server-id>, and configure its access policy for this client. Do not assume /oauth2/default exists in every deployment; see authorization servers. Additional required claims must actually be emitted for this client and scope.

items.title: authentik
items.text:
Unverified with altero. Create an application and an OAuth2/OIDC provider using the provider wizard. Choose a confidential client, set the exact callback as a strict redirect URI, and select the openid, profile and email scope mappings. Copy the client ID and secret into altero; leave token encryption disabled.

Keep the default per-provider issuer mode and a stable subject identifier. Set altero's Issuer to https://<authentik-host>/application/o/<application-slug>/, including the final slash. Copy the actual value from discovery. Global issuer mode uses a different discovery location from its issuer and does not fit altero's issuer-based discovery. See authentik's issuer modes and endpoints. Configure application access bindings and any required claim for your policy.

items.title: Shibboleth IdP
items.text:
Unverified with altero. Use SAML 2.0. Give the IdP administrator the entity ID and HTTP-POST ACS above, and register the service provider in its metadata. Altero does not publish a metadata endpoint; this minimal descriptor is a starting point, with your own host and short name substituted:

<EntityDescriptor xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:metadata"
                  entityID="https://library.example.org">
  <SPSSODescriptor protocolSupportEnumeration="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol"
                   AuthnRequestsSigned="false" WantAssertionsSigned="true">
    <NameIDFormat>urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:persistent</NameIDFormat>
    <AssertionConsumerService Binding="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:bindings:HTTP-POST"
        Location="https://library.example.org/web/auth/saml/shibboleth/acs"
        index="0" isDefault="true"/>
  </SPSSODescriptor>
</EntityDescriptor>

Enable a persistent NameID generator before the first sign-in; a transient NameID changes the identity between sessions. For this relying party, use the SAML2.SSO profile with signAssertions="true", encryptAssertions="false" and encryptNameIDs="false", and accept unsigned AuthnRequests. Apply these choices only to altero's relying party; see signing/encryption settings and SAML 2.0 profile options.

Copy the IdP entity ID, HTTP-Redirect sign-on URL and signing certificate from its metadata into altero. Arrange release of username, display-name and email attributes. If their Name or FriendlyName values are eppn, displayName and mail, use those as altero's three claim names; otherwise use the actual released names. Altero reads attributes from the signed assertion and makes no separate attribute-query request.

items.title: Check a configuration
items.text:
Use a test account to sign in twice, signing out of altero between attempts. Both visits should reach the same local account. For an existing account with creation disabled, test linking from Settings first. Confirm that the provider also supports a fresh sign-in when Settings asks for proof to issue an API key.

If using a required claim, test both an allowed and a denied identity. Losing that claim after linking suspends the local account at its next sign-in; restoring the claim alone does not reinstate it. An administrator must reinstate the account. This is still a sign-in-time check, not continuous deprovisioning. See account creation and deprovisioning.

items.title: Third-party applications
items.text:
Register applications that should receive limited, expiring library access. Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL first, then use:

uv run altero oauth add notebook \
    --name "Notebook" \
    --redirect-uri https://notebook.example.com/auth/callback \
    --scope openid --scope profile --scope library.read
uv run altero oauth list
uv run altero oauth disable notebook

Account holders approve access in their browsers and can disconnect an application under Settings → Connected applications. See Connecting other applications for scopes, registration and developer details.

items.title: Retention
items.text:
Retention starts conservatively: the default trash-retention period is never delete automatically.

Configuration values:

TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS = 0
ACTIVITY_RETENTION_DAYS = 0
UPLOAD_RETENTION_HOURS = 24
RETENTION_INTERVAL = 0

0 means “no automatic retention action” for the day-based settings and interval. Browser-configured values override the configuration file; clearing a browser override returns to the configured value.

Inspect and run retention from the shell:

uv run altero retention show
uv run altero retention run --dry-run
uv run altero retention run --dry-run --trash 30
uv run altero retention run

items.title: What cleanup removes
items.text:
Trash cleanup permanently deletes eligible objects and records the deletions for syncing clients. It checks again for items restored or changed during the sweep. Age is measured from the last server-recorded item change, rather than a separate time of trashing.

The sweep also removes expired sessions, codes, links, invitations, download permissions and private undo snapshots. These have their own expiry times.

Unreferenced attachment files require a separate cleanup action in Storage; timed retention does not remove them. A grace period protects files belonging to uploads still in progress.

items.title: Move a library to another altero instance
items.text:
Export the library:

uv run altero library export user 1 library.zip

On the destination, create the owning account or group first, then import:

uv run altero user add <username> --id 1
uv run altero library import library.zip

The archive contains JSON metadata and attachment bytes, including object keys, object versions, the library version and the deletion log. Accounts and API keys are not included.

Exporting holds library writes until the archive is built, so its contents describe one consistent version. The lock is released before downloading. Restoring also locks the target library before checking or replacing its contents.

Importing into a non-empty target is refused unless --replace is used.

The browser exposes equivalent import/export operations under Settings → Import and export.

items.title: Move a personal library from zotero.org
items.text:
This is a one-time migration. It does not keep the two servers synchronized afterwards. Finish syncing to zotero.org before importing, and pause edits until the clients have moved to altero. Continuous two-way sync is unsupported; a scheduled one-way refresh is future work. See the verdict and replacement-import limits.

If possible, create the altero account with the same numeric user ID that zotero.org uses:

uv run altero user add <username> --id <zotero.org-user-id>
uv run altero migrate zotero <username> --replace

The migration asks for a zotero.org API key with read access to the personal library. The key is prompted for rather than placed on the command line.

The migration preserves Zotero object keys and versions so an already-synchronized desktop client can continue from the same state.

If the account numbers differ, linking the existing profile is refused. Use an account with the original number or a fresh profile, as explained in A profile that has synced before.

Only the personal library is imported. Attachment bytes that zotero.org does not hold cannot be downloaded; the migration lists those items and brings the attachments across without their files.

Important

If attachment files were synchronized over WebDAV, zotero.org holds none of them. It answers 404 for every one, so the whole library arrives without files. The metadata is complete: item keys, md5 and mtime are all preserved. Either keep the WebDAV server for files, or move the files into altero from a client that still has them. See File syncing.

items.title: After recreating the database
items.text:
Pause other clients before recovery. A desktop may remember a later library version than a recreated database or older archive. Raising the server's library version fixes that counter mismatch, but does not make older item versions replace newer desktop caches.

If a surviving desktop holds the complete authoritative library:

  1. Back up its data directory and the server before proceeding.
  2. Raise the server library version above the value remembered by that desktop:
uv run altero library set-version user 1 <higher-version>
  1. Use Zotero's Restore to Server to upload the surviving desktop's complete copy.
  2. Verify metadata and attachment bytes before reconnecting other clients.

This command only raises the counter; it recreates no lost objects or files. Do not resume normal sync assuming the version change restored data. Without a complete surviving copy, restore from a verified backup and plan how each client will obtain that state. Automatic rewind of synced desktop objects is unsupported.

items.title: Group policy
items.text:
A group has three Zotero-compatible policy settings:

Setting Values Controls libraryReading members, all Who may read the library libraryEditing members, admins Who may edit objects fileEditing none, members, admins Who may upload attachment files

The group type is Private, PublicOpen or PublicClosed.

A public group is readable without a key only when the group is public and libraryReading is all.

Membership remains a ceiling over key permissions: a key that grants access to all groups still cannot read a group the account does not belong to.

items.title: Per-member permissions
items.text:
altero can apply an additional restriction to one member:

Permission Meaning inherit Use the normal group policy read Read only add Create and change, but do not remove or trash own Create freely; change or remove only items that member added

From the shell:

uv run altero group member <group> <username> --permission read
uv run altero group permission <group> <username> add
uv run altero group members <group>

These permissions can only restrict what the group policy already allows. They do not elevate a member above the group's normal policy.

Only the read-only state maps cleanly onto a permission the Zotero sync client understands. add and own are enforced server-side; a client that attempts a forbidden operation receives a sync error explaining the restriction. See Compatibility notes.

items.title: Checking desktop compatibility
items.text:
Run the optional compatibility suite when changing responses or versions that Zotero Desktop consumes. It feeds altero API responses into original desktop functions, and inventories source expectations to find contracts worth testing.

Choose the check that matches the change:

Check Evidence Source discovery Candidate omissions and network consumers to review Source replay Original desktop methods consuming altero responses Generated sequences State invariants across ordered operations Desktop acceptance Actual profiles, sync engine, dialogs and files Mutations Whether assertions detect deliberate defects

The normal Python suite needs neither Node nor a desktop checkout. This optional toolchain needs Node matching tools/compatibility/package.json, its own parser installation, and the source revision in tools/compatibility/contracts.toml. The installed desktop binary is pinned independently in desktop.toml.

items.title: Set up the checkout
items.text:
From the altero repository root, install the parser and clone a separate desktop checkout:

npm --prefix tools/compatibility ci
git clone https://github.com/zotero/zotero.git .compatibility/zotero
uv run python - <<'PY'
import subprocess
import tomllib
from pathlib import Path
manifest = tomllib.loads(Path("tools/compatibility/contracts.toml").read_text())
subprocess.run(
    ["git", "-C", ".compatibility/zotero", "checkout", manifest["zotero"]["revision"]],
    check=True,
)
PY

An existing clean checkout at that revision works too; substitute its path in the commands below. Verification checks the commit, tracked changes, complete source-file fingerprints, and function selectors:

uv run python -m tools.compatibility verify --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero
uv run pytest -q compatibility_tests --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero

ALTERO_ZOTERO_SOURCE supplies the test suite's default path. Missing source, Node, dependencies, or selectors fail the checks rather than skipping them. The ignored .compatibility/ directory holds checkouts and generated reports.

items.title: What the executable contracts cover
items.text:
Contract Original desktop code Behavior checked Group permissions getPermissionsFromJSON Members, administrators, group policies, files and read-only restrictions, through both group endpoints Group refresh checkLibraries and Group.fromJSON A cached client fetches changed permissions after an API or command-line change moves the advertised version Group listing getGroups, getPaginatedResults, _parseLinkHeader Empty, single-page and multiple-page results remain readable in account preferences Sync versions getVersions and _parseJSON A version listing carries its watermark, and a 304 is accepted without a body Live sync reads API key, settings, deletion, keys, versions and object-download methods Personal and group libraries, restricted key flags, Unicode, incremental reads, trash, parent/child objects, missing keys and 99/100/101-object download batches Live sync writes Object/settings uploads and deletions Mixed successful/unchanged/failed results, stale library and object versions, absent versus empty properties, trash/restore/delete sequences, deletion logs, 49/50/51-object writes and recovery after a committed write loses its response Schema corpus Generated from the vendored schema, through original API downloads All 40 item types, every listed field and creator role, Unicode, client timestamps, notes, attachments and annotations HTTP policy Original request and retry methods Backoff, numeric and invalid Retry-After, increasing 429 delays, terminal errors and connection loss after a committed write; delays use a virtual clock Full text Full-text upload, read and version methods Empty and Unicode content, client-selected gzip, missing content, incremental versions and stale writes Files Original ZFS transfer methods Authorization, unauthenticated byte upload, registration, absolute download locations, MD5/mtime/compression metadata, ZIP snapshots and unchanged-file download avoidance

The desktop sends partial object changes inside a POST batch. Its API helper also accepts a PATCH method argument, but the sync engine uses POST and the dataserver does not accept PATCH on the collection endpoint for items. The field-clearing scenarios therefore exercise partial POST bodies.

The child-demotion acceptance scenario makes a standalone PDF into a child and verifies that collection memberships are removed and both profiles settle. This protects against a desktop foreign-key failure on invalid child membership.

Source selectors identify original JavaScript functions. Adapters provide HTTP, persistence and file facades while retaining the selected decision logic. DesktopAPI runs the original API client over live HTTP; DesktopStorage runs its file-transfer methods. Subprocess calls remain asynchronous so the server can answer them.

These facades do not prove generic HTTP retries, desktop disk writes or ZIP unpacking. Actual desktop acceptance supplies that evidence separately.

Duplicate merging has service, HTTP, browser and desktop checks. They cover field choices, relations, permissions, rollback, stale reviews, attachment matching, notes and annotation parents. PDF extraction uses a different parser from Zotero, so matching arbitrary PDFs is not guaranteed. Extraction failures are treated conservatively as possible embedded markup. The browser merge contract is documented in implementation notes.

Source replay and real desktop scenarios are separate inventory entries; neither should stand in for the other.

items.title: Discover contracts from source
items.text:
The network inventory scans all JavaScript and modules under the pinned desktop's chrome/content and resource trees, including JSX, anonymous callbacks and file-level requests. It includes HTTP helpers, file downloads, fetch, XHR and WebSocket construction. Every discovered consumer has a fingerprinted review in tools/compatibility/interactions.json: supported with test references, pending, unsupported, external service, or general transport. A changed source file, removed consumer, parse error or new consumer fails the review gate:

.venv/bin/python -m tools.compatibility interactions \
  --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero --check \
  --output .compatibility/interactions.json --markdown .compatibility/interactions.md

The inventory is syntactic, not a whole-program call graph. Dynamic URLs and unresolved options stay visible for review. Supported library sync, unsupported services, external services and general transport each retain their disposition. Runtime traces omit credential values and login/storage tokens in paths.

An inventory entry records scope, not a successful run.

Inspect the scenario inventory before extending coverage:

uv run python -m tools.compatibility coverage \
  --output .compatibility/coverage.json --markdown .compatibility/coverage.md

tools/compatibility/surface.toml records executable, pending, desktop-runtime and deliberately unsupported scenarios. Executable means test code exists; the test run supplies the result. Counts describe scenarios, not a percentage of API compatibility. Discovery also scans item, collection and search serialization and the streaming client.

uv run python -m tools.compatibility analyze \
  --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero \
  --output .compatibility/report.json \
  --markdown .compatibility/report.md \
  --evidence .compatibility/evidence.json

The report compares mapped client field reads with possible server response shapes and retains source positions, unmapped consumers and parse errors.

Status Meaning candidate No known emission for a client-read field; reproduce the effect no-static-gap Static fields match; behavior still needs tests execution-only Executable check without static field comparison unresolved Dynamic shape or source prevents comparison

Presence does not establish correct values or permissions. Zero candidates therefore does not establish compatibility. Discovery reports findings without failing; exit 2 indicates unusable prerequisites or runner/output errors.

items.title: Add automated source review
items.text:
The evidence JSON is also the input to an optional review program. It includes mapped consumer/provider code, conditions, known exceptions, and unmapped consumers with any matched routes. Source bodies share a 64,000-character budget; clipped blocks are marked truncated.

To invoke a reviewer of your choosing:

uv run python -m tools.compatibility analyze \
  --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero \
  --review-command 'your-review-program' \
  --output .compatibility/review.json \
  --markdown .compatibility/review.md

The program reads one JSON object from stdin and writes this shape to stdout:

{
  "findings": [{
    "contract": "group_permissions",
    "summary": "A hypothesis about the client and server behavior",
    "client": {"file": "chrome/content/zotero/xpcom/data/groups.js", "line": 138},
    "server": {"file": "src/altero/serializers.py", "line": 109},
    "reproduction": "Setup, action, and expected client behavior"
  }]
}

Use contract: null for an unmapped consumer. References must fall within the supplied source spans. Invalid output and process failures are reported; every accepted finding stays unverified. The command receives a JSON protocol and can wrap a local analyzer or a model service. No model provider is built in or called by the default workflow, and generated tests or fixes are never executed by this interface.

items.title: Add a contract or update Zotero
items.text:
1. Establish the behavior using the project's compatibility reference and contributing rules. Record any deliberate exception with its reason.
  2. Add the consumer's source path, unique selector, complete file SHA-256, server binding and test path to the manifest. server.input names the consumer parameter and server.object the response object to compare. Additional evidence entries supply related server functions.
  3. Write a scenario using actual endpoint responses and the original function. Supply only the runtime facades it needs in adapters.mjs.
  4. Prove the check fails with the defect restored. Test transitions as well as fresh responses when the client caches a decision.

For a new desktop revision, first run discovery against a separate checkout with --allow-source-drift. The report marks mismatched revisions or fingerprints as unpinned. Review the changed functions and adapters before updating the manifest's commit and hashes together, then run verification and every contract. This flag is for discovery; executable checks always enforce their fingerprints.

items.title: CI reports
items.text:
The Desktop compatibility workflow verifies pinned sources, replays contracts and rejects skips. Reports include source discovery, reference evidence, scenario inventory and test results. Nightly/manual checks also inspect upstream source with drift allowed and run mutations without changing the supported pin.

Real desktop acceptance runs separately under Xvfb. CI checks the Linux archive hash and running version from desktop.toml and preserves reports, logs and databases on failure. Scheduled jobs and successful downloads are not passing acceptance results; use the recorded matrix.

items.title: Cross-check the dataserver reference
items.text:
Pass --dataserver-source /path/to/dataserver to verify and analyze. tools/compatibility/reference.toml pins the independent reference revision, complete source hashes and reviewed PHP spans for group pagination, write results and limits, partial batches, deletions, settings, full text and storage. Verification fails on revision, tracked changes, hashes or invalid spans. The report includes the source comparison and the review packet includes bounded reference evidence. PHP is inspected, not executed; this is not a live api.zotero.org differential test.

The comparison records two deliberate differences relevant to these scenarios: altero substitutes a self Link for upstream's zotero.org alternate, and retains one library version per changed request, while this dataserver revision bumps per object and commits a bump for unchanged objects. Full-text versioning already has the same documented per-request distinction. Compare object state and monotonic watermarks rather than expecting equal counter values.

items.title: Generated sequences and replay
items.text:
Sequences use a fresh loopback server, database and file store. Existing state directories are refused. The independent model checks effective create, edit, file, unfile, trash, restore and delete operations after each step.

Failures shrink on fresh servers while retaining the invariant's object family, key and field. Invalid or ineffective sequences do not count as reproductions. Reports preserve original and minimized operations. Exit 1 means an assertion failure; runner and prerequisite failures use exit 2.

Run and replay a standalone sequence with preserved disposable databases:

uv run python -m tools.compatibility sequence --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero \
  --seed 14 --steps 30 --state-dir .compatibility/sequence-14 \
  --output .compatibility/sequence-14.json
uv run python -m tools.compatibility sequence --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero \
  --replay .compatibility/sequence-14.json --state-dir .compatibility/replay-14 \
  --output .compatibility/replay-14.json

Use --model protocol --steps 60 for the broader model covering object graphs, settings, files, full text, deletions, permissions and two offline patch queues:

uv run python -m tools.compatibility sequence --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero \
  --model protocol --seed 14 --steps 60 --state-dir .compatibility/protocol-14 \
  --output .compatibility/protocol-14.json

Replay selects the recorded model automatically. Shrinking rejects orphaned children, collection cycles, denied writes, stranded work and no-op operations. The queued-patch policy belongs to this harness, not Zotero's desktop engine.

items.title: Run two real desktop profiles
items.text:
Acceptance runs two isolated desktop profiles against a disposable server, using the actual sync engine and file storage. Supply an installed executable and its exact version; use the archive pin in desktop.toml for reproducible CI comparisons.

uv run python -m tools.compatibility acceptance \
  --desktop-executable /path/to/zotero --desktop-version <installed-version> \
  --xvfb --schema-corpus --state-dir .compatibility/desktop-run

Use a fresh state directory. --xvfb requires Xvfb; omit it for an existing display. Each profile gets its own temporary directory and waits for schema and bundled-file initialization. The add-on applies operations through original Zotero APIs without replacing sync or conflict dialogs.

For PostgreSQL, add --postgres-url postgresql+asyncpg://altero:altero@localhost:55432/altero. The account must be able to create databases. Each scenario creates and retains a fresh database; its name is saved in server/database.json without credentials. The database named in the URL is not migrated. Without this option, SQLite state stays in the run directory.

Repeat --scenario to select cases; the default runs all implemented scenarios. The top-level acceptance.json and scenario directories retain snapshots and logs, including on failure.

Core scenario Coverage baseline Parent/child objects, schema types, attachment bytes, offline edits, trash and deletion conflicts Actual local/remote choices, edit/delete conflicts, cancellation and recovery filing Concurrent tag and collection additions groups Role/policy changes, permission-loss choices, archival, removal and rejoining files Replacement, both file-conflict choices, missing-file recovery and snapshot unpacking relationships Collection moves, reparenting, type changes, searches and annotations recovery Interrupted desktop requests and downloads, restart and concurrent pending work credentials Login helpers, revocation, relinking and account-mismatch cancellation

The convergence check compares all pages of persisted objects, child graphs, fields, significant list ordering, pending work and downloaded bytes. Matching titles alone is insufficient. Desktop item versions may exceed server object versions because the client stamps a batch watermark. lastRead is normalized numerically; setting values and finished queues must match even where setting version metadata differs.

File-conflict tests use different displayed modification dates. Equal-date selection has a recorded client defect and is not covered by a passing distinct-date scenario. Missing files are recovered through the original on-demand download rather than forced storage flags.

Source replay of streaming handlers uses a socket facade and virtual clock. The streaming-reconnect acceptance scenario separately checks actual sockets, resubscription and notification-driven sync.

items.title: Additional desktop scenarios
items.text:
Each scenario uses two actual desktop profiles, original desktop operations, real HTTP, persistent databases and files. Unexpected sync errors fail the run. The final settled sync checks convergence and an unchanged server watermark.

Scenario Assertions fulltext Index an isolated HTML snapshot; upload and download the index; search ASCII, Unicode and CJK terms in B without downloading the attachment; preserve the index across restart. read-races Hold actual settings, top-version, object-batch and deletion responses; edit remotely while B has pending local work; verify download-cycle restart, unseen edits and pending uploads. settings Concurrent tag-color edits and ordering; original settings conflict policy; deletion followed by recreation while B is offline; persisted values and the tag-color cache. partial-failures A mixed group upload succeeds for one object and refuses owner-created parent and child edits with exactly two 403 errors; pending work survives and uploads after permission is restored. graphs Merge duplicate parents and retain children and relations; publish with CC0 and withdraw; copy notes and attachment bytes into a group; repeat the original copy without duplicates. http-policy Induce a real server 429; let the original desktop HTTP policy retry; upload once and converge without continued version changes. server-writes Make collection, filing, tag and trash changes through the browser's authenticated HTTP routes; execute the real retention sweep; observe changes and deletion logs in both desktops. web-editing Edit an item's fields, creators and tags, relate two items, change a type and make an item through the browser's routes; both desktops store exactly that; a desktop edit then makes the browser's stale save fail with 412. web-undo Trash and file a selection through the browser, then undo after both desktops have synced; preserve prior memberships, preexisting trash and child-note HTML/parents; a real desktop edit invalidates a stale undo. web-copy-undo Copy a parent, note and registered file into a group; sync both desktops before undo; keep the copied graph and bytes recoverable through Trash/Restore, and preserve the originals. web-merge-undo Merge two PDFs with embedded notes and an annotation; sync both desktops before undo; restore original metadata, links, memberships, note HTML and parents, trash promoted notes and retain file bytes. note-corpus Store notes as clients wrote them, from TinyMCE-era HTML to schema 10 and a note built from PDF annotations; have the shipped note editor save each unedited; record both for the browser editor's tests, and check the server keeps the desktop's HTML exactly. web-notes Write a standalone and a child note through the browser's routes; both desktops store exactly that HTML; the desktop's editor opens them editable and writes nothing; a desktop edit reaches the browser. web-files Upload a child and a standalone file and attach a web link through the browser's routes; both desktops download the bytes under the browser's name; a rename renames each desktop's copy without fetching it; a replacement brings new bytes; a desktop's replacement makes the browser's stale one fail with 412. web-merge Merge through the browser route; both desktops retain chosen fields, moved notes and links, tags, collections, incoming relations and replacement history; refuse a stale review; restore the duplicate record without reversing the merge. web-merge-files Match PDFs by bytes or extracted text, retain embedded markup, preserve notes and annotation parents, keep both files when needed for safe parent sync, and verify original bytes and settled storage on both desktops. resync Discard pending edits through the original reset helper; replace the server from a desktop; restore an older server archive, lift its watermark and recover from the surviving authoritative desktop. file-lifecycle Rename Unicode filenames; reuse a stored digest and delete one reference; recover a missing local file; refuse a stale download redirect with 404, observe the expected storage failure, then recover current bytes and hashes. upload-interruption Kill the desktop process group while the server has consumed only part of a large incompressible upload; assert no premature registration; restart and compare complete bytes and settled storage states. server-crash SIGKILL a separate serving process after an item commit but before its response; kill the waiting desktop, restart the server on the same database and URL, and recover without duplicate objects or versions. graph-races Reparent a note and delete its former parent while top-version, object-batch and deletion responses are held; preserve unrelated pending work and converge without resurrecting the parent. credential-limits Expire and cancel actual login sessions through original desktop methods; remove a key's personal-library read access while offline work is pending, restore access and upload that work. transient-errors Real 503s before and after a write, a lost commit response, a truncated object read, and user cancellation through the original sync runner; recover without duplicates or extra versions. streaming-reconnect Close the actual WebSocket with 1012, observe the original two-second reconnect delay and resubscription, then send a notification that drives automatic desktop sync without an explicit sync call.

HTTP barriers hold genuine requests independently. A fault before execution performs no write; a response fault can lose an already committed answer. Partial download and upload failures use incomplete transport bodies. Crash checks restart the same database and URL and compare durable state and retry preconditions. A consumed file-registration token returns 404 on retry; current metadata and downloaded bytes establish recovery.

Process interruption terminates the entire isolated desktop process group. Barrier traces redact credentials. These controls exist only in the disposable harness. Socket-level durable-write checks remain distinct from desktop acceptance.

Seven further cases cover additional transitions:

Scenario Coverage parent-rejection Rejected parent and dependent 409, unrelated success, displayed errors and retry missing-parent A synced parent missing on the server is requeued from the child's 409 child-promotion parentItem: false makes a child top-level on both desktops type-change Fields and creator roles map to a different item type reader-rendering Actual PDF canvas pixels, changed PNG cache after crop and restart persistence zipped-digest-race Concurrent uploads with equal main-file digests and different ZIPs; archive integrity and unpacked resources backup-rewind A raised watermark does not rewind desktop objects; explicit surviving-client recovery

Browser-route scenarios use real sessions and CSRF tokens, but do not establish browser sign-in UI coverage. Automatic rewind remains unsupported. More platforms, credential combinations, reader formats and failure schedules need separate evidence.

items.title: Prove the checks detect omissions
items.text:
uv run python -m tools.compatibility mutations --zotero-source .compatibility/zotero \
  --state-dir .compatibility/mutations --output .compatibility/mutations.json

Seven named mutations remove a watermark, truncate versions, omit a successful write result, omit a deletion, ignore empty clearing properties, freeze the watermark or remove the group roster. Every canary first has to pass intact, then fail by assertion in every parametrized case. Setup errors, skips and unrelated exceptions are rejected. JUnit and logs are preserved for each run. All seven were detected locally, including PR #14's missing-roster class.

These are controlled protocol mutations at the transport boundary. The clearing mutation removes empty properties before sending the request, simulating a writer that ignores them; the others alter responses. They establish assertion strength, not a mutation score for production source. ALTERO_COMPAT_MUTATION selects only a catalogue entry and is normally unset.

Results above are local executions with the pinned Linux x86-64 Zotero 10.0.7 archive on Python 3.14.10. The original 36 scenarios ran on each database on 2026-10-30 against the beta.7 release candidate, including the 15-phase schema baseline. Not run means there is no successful result recorded for that combination; executable inventory entries and scheduled CI jobs do not count as passes.

The additional web-undo scenario passed on both databases on 2026-11-02, with 15 phases each against the current checkout. Both desktops downloaded filing and trash changes before undo, then converged on the restored state; a subsequent desktop edit made an old undo fail with 412. Its separate evidence summary records report and phase-snapshot hashes.

web-copy-undo also passed on both databases on 2026-11-02, with 14 phases each. Both desktops downloaded a browser-made group copy before undo and retained its note and registered bytes through Trash/Restore. The original personal-library records and files remained intact, and settled sync preserved both libraries' watermarks. Its evidence summary records the reports and phase-snapshot hashes.

web-merge-undo passed on both databases on 2026-11-03, with 11 phases each. Both desktops received a merge of two PDFs with embedded notes and an annotation before Undo restored the original content, dates added, parent links, tags, collections and relations. Promoted notes went to Trash, both original PDF files remained intact, and the next sync preserved the library watermark. The fixture forces duplicate restoration before its survivor's update, exercising Zotero's automatic merge-link cleanup and the preservation of relation-only modification dates. It also verifies clearing the last creator reaches both desktop caches. The evidence summary records report and phase-snapshot hashes. These are local Linux checks; the scenario is also included in the scheduled/manual PostgreSQL CI matrix. No hosted run or non-Linux execution is claimed for this addition.

The machine-readable evidence summary is compatibility-10.0.7.json. It records phase counts and SHA-256 hashes of each report and its phase snapshots. Retained reports, profiles, files and failed attempts live in ignored local run directories. Regenerate the matrix from them with:

uv run python -m tools.compatibility matrix --desktop-version 10.0.7 \
  --report .compatibility/beta7-10.0.7-sqlite-1/acceptance.json \
  --report .compatibility/beta7-10.0.7-pg-1/acceptance.json \
  --output .compatibility/results.json --markdown .compatibility/matrix.md

The command verifies scenario completion, nonempty phases, snapshot existence, the requested desktop version and recorded database backend. It rejects missing or mismatched evidence. Interrupted phases retain their process exit status; completed phases identify their running binary. Summary hashes are evidence identifiers, not signatures or a certification of the whole desktop surface.

The original 2026-10-30 run recorded 72 database/scenario combinations and 838 phases across 36 scenarios. Later undo scenarios are recorded separately above. The baseline includes all 40 schema types. The 2026-10-30 source-replay run passed 333 tests with no skips against the pinned 10.0.7 sources, with Node 24.22.1; its network-consumer review gate had no stale or unreviewed consumers. Regressions cover the restore request marker and reconnecting after WebSocket close 4429; both fail against the older source.

The earlier 10.0.6 browser-merge checks also ran with deliberate omissions after their intact baselines passed. Missing replacement history failed at Desktop merge history is missing after five phases; disabling PDF text matching failed at Incorrect surviving PDFs for matching-text after seven. Those failed runs and the restored-source hashes are retained locally.

Two harness defects surfaced while moving to 10.0.6 and are fixed: profiles followed the machine's language, so a German system showed prompts the dialog rules could not find, and Zotero's automatic update could replace a pinned binary between phases. Profiles now request English and turn automatic updates off. The PHP dataserver and browser sign-in UI were not executed. The desktop evidence is Linux-only; exhaustive credential combinations, reader formats and failure schedules remain unverified.

items.title: Recorded client behavior
items.text:
Equal displayed file-conflict dates exposed a client defect: selecting Remote can keep and upload local bytes. It was reproduced with Zotero 10.0.1, and with 10.0.6 against Zotero Storage on 2026-10-30. The upstream report records dialog selection, hashes and a passing different-date control. This case has not been rerun on 10.0.7; its acceptance run used distinct dates.

PDF parent/note merging also reproduced a Zotero 10.0.6 defect against zotero.org and offline: a changed note could persist while its parent move was lost. altero retains both PDFs when that combination would occur; see the compatibility decision.

items.title: Connecting a Zotero client
items.text:
This page describes how to connect an unmodified Zotero Desktop installation to altero.

Automated desktop acceptance has run on Linux. Windows and macOS have a community basic-sync report, with broader coverage still unverified; see platform status and testing instructions.

Before you begin: use a test profile or a library you can recreate.

items.title: Configure Zotero Desktop
items.text:
Open Settings → Advanced → Config Editor and set both preferences:

extensions.zotero.api.url = http://localhost:8000/
extensions.zotero.streaming.url = ws://localhost:8000/stream

The trailing slash on extensions.zotero.api.url matters.

For a server behind TLS, use https:// for the API and wss:// for streaming.

Important

api.url does not redirect the streaming connection. If extensions.zotero.streaming.url is left unchanged, Zotero falls back to its built-in wss://stream.zotero.org endpoint and may send the altero API key there. zotero.org rejects that key, but the key may appear in upstream logs.

If you do not want streaming updates, disable streaming explicitly:

extensions.zotero.streaming.enabled = false

Restart Zotero after changing the preferences.

items.title: Link the account
items.text:
In Zotero, open Settings → Sync → Link Account.

Use the browser window Zotero opens to sign in and approve the connection. Zotero receives an API key that covers the account's personal and group libraries.

Approval requires fresh identity confirmation. Enter your password when asked, or use Confirm with <provider> for a provider-linked account without a password. Complete the approval within five minutes of provider confirmation. On an institutional-only instance, confirmation always uses the provider.

items.title: A profile that has synced before
items.text:
Zotero remembers the numeric account id its data directory last synced under, and sends it when linking. altero refuses to hand a key to a different account, because the desktop client reacts to a changed id by offering to reset the data directory and quitting.

If the remembered account number differs from your altero account number, linking is refused and the message names the expected number.

To continue:

  • Create the account with that id. altero user add <username> --id <id> gives the profile the account it is asking for, and it carries on. This is also what moving a personal library from zotero.org relies on.
  • Link from a data directory that has never synced. A fresh Zotero profile sends no id. Nothing is carried over by doing this; the old library stays where it is.

items.title: File syncing
items.text: Attachment files are configured separately from library data, in Settings → Sync → File Syncing. There, Zotero means altero, because extensions.zotero.api.url points at it. Group libraries always sync their files through altero; WebDAV cannot carry them.

items.title: Keeping an existing WebDAV server
items.text:
Leave Sync attachment files in My Library using WebDAV unchanged. altero then carries the library data and the WebDAV server keeps carrying the files.

A personal library migrated from zotero.org keeps its item keys and each attachment's md5 and mtime, so the <KEY>.zip and <KEY>.prop files already on the WebDAV server still match.

items.title: Moving files from WebDAV into altero
items.text:
Files stored on WebDAV are never present on zotero.org, so a migration cannot bring them across. Move them from a client whose Zotero data directory still holds them:

Warning

This uploads the whole attachment store in one sync. altero accepts up to 1 GiB per file by default (ALTERO_MAX_UPLOAD_MB); a reverse proxy needs its own request-size limit raised, as described under Behind a reverse proxy.

  1. Set Settings → Sync → File Syncing → Sync attachment files in My Library using Zotero.
  2. Open Settings → Sync → Sync Reset → Show Reset Options…, select the library, and run Reset File Sync History.
  3. Sync.

Step 2 is required. Zotero otherwise treats the files as already synchronized, because the migrated attachments carry the same md5 and mtime the WebDAV server recorded, and uploads nothing. The reset marks every attachment whose file is present locally for upload.

An attachment whose file no longer exists anywhere stays a metadata-only item. altero answers 404 for its bytes, and Zotero records it as in sync rather than reporting an error.

items.title: Command-line approval
items.text:
If the browser interface is not built, the same login can be approved from the server shell:

uv run altero login list
uv run altero login approve <token> <username>

login approve creates a key unless you supply an existing one with --key.

items.title: Test with two desktop clients
items.text:
Two Zotero installations on one machine can use separate profiles and data directories. This is useful for testing whether changes really travel through the server rather than only exercising one side of sync.

See Syncing two desktop clients.

items.title: Mobile apps
items.text:
The official iOS and Android apps have no setting for a different server. They need a separate build that sends both API and streaming traffic to altero; altero does not distribute one.

For Android, the third-party zotero-self-hosted-sync patch bundle can change those addresses. Check its README for supported app releases. It is not maintained or reviewed by altero and will hold your API key.

App Evidence Android Sync and file uploads reported working on a device with a redirected build iOS Checked against source; no device test recorded

This route is unofficial, but protocol differences from zotero.org are worth reporting. Sign-in uses browser approval as on the desktop.

items.title: Compatibility reference
items.text:
Use this reference when integrating a client or investigating behavior that differs from Zotero's published API documentation. Each decision describes the observable result and its reason.

altero targets unmodified Zotero Desktop. Where documentation disagrees with behavior clients depend on, compatibility wins. Evidence includes the live API, the reference dataserver and real-client checks. Inferences and untested behavior are marked explicitly.

For setup and ordinary use, start with Clients or the web guide.

items.title: Omitted note content in partial writes
items.text: A partial write that leaves out note keeps the existing note text, for notes and attachments alike. Sending note: "" clears it. A full replacement (PUT) still replaces everything. This matches the dataserver, which only touches the note when the property is present.

items.title: Empty creators in item responses
items.text: Regular items include creators: [] when empty. Omitting it from a sync response makes an existing desktop retain its previous creators. Notes, attachments and annotations have no creator list.

items.title: Racing ZIP archives of different sizes
items.text:
When the client uploads a web snapshot, md5 describes the file inside the archive and zipMD5 the archive itself. Two clients zipping the same snapshot produce archives of different sizes with the same md5.

Each archive is stored under its own zipMD5, as on zotero.org, so neither replaces the other: both registrations succeed, and each attachment downloads the archive its own client sent.

items.title: Search syntax
items.text:
The itemType and tag parameters behave differently from what the documentation suggests, in two ways that change results.

Negation covers the whole value. itemType=-book || journalArticle excludes both types; it does not mean "not a book, or a journal article". This was confirmed by counting against a real library of 442 items: itemType=attachment || note matched 134 and itemType=-attachment || note returned exactly 308.

|| only separates when there is whitespace on both sides. tag=a||b is one tag literally named a||b, and so is tag=a ||b. This lets a tag containing || round-trip. Every documented example uses the spaced form, so clients are unaffected.

A leading hyphen is escaped as \-. Only the whole value is trimmed, once, so inner spacing in tag=foo bar || bar survives.

items.title: Quick search and full-text search
items.text:
Quick search combines words with AND across the title, note title, creators and year. Double quotes group a phrase; single quotes do not. As upstream, unquoted q=0 applies no filter, while q="0" searches for zero.

With qmode=everything, altero also searches stored attachment text and every item field. It uses database substring matching instead of a separate search service. The differences are:

  • Character substrings match: equod finds Pequod. Punctuation can interrupt a phrase match.
  • Accents are significant; case is ignored across alphabets. Chinese and Japanese terms require consecutive characters.
  • % and _ act as wildcards. Terms shorter than three characters require a slower scan.
  • All fields are searched, including fields upstream omits.
  • There is no upstream-style 300-hit full-text cap.

Upstream's documented analyzer defaults imply different word and phrase behavior; that analyzer comparison is an inference, not a direct measurement.

/top returns the parent of a matching child for q, tag, itemKey and itemType. All words must match the same item. since does not promote a child to its parent. Neither a trashed match nor a trashed parent is returned.

Tag-name search is case-sensitive: /tags?q=fic does not find Fiction. It also accepts % and _ wildcards, escaped with a backslash when literal.

items.title: Tag counts and the trash
items.text:
Library-wide /tags counts include trashed items, even with includeTrashed=0. A tag carried only by trashed items remains listed. This matches reviewed upstream behavior (dataserver#51); it is source evidence, not a new live measurement.

Use /items/tags for live-item counts or /items/trash/tags for Trash. includeTrashed=1 widens the former. Collection scopes and restricted OAuth grants still limit which items are counted. The browser uses item-scoped counts.

items.title: Who added an item, and who last changed it
items.text:
In group libraries, an item's meta names who created it and who last changed it. Both behaviors below are copied, including the parts that look like oversights.

  • Group libraries only. createdByUser and lastModifiedByUser never appear in a personal library, where there is only one person.
  • lastModifiedByUser is left out when it is the same person as createdByUser. The common case — somebody adds an item and then fixes its title — shows one name, not the same name twice.
  • The name shown is the person's real name, or their username when they have none.
  • No alternate link to a profile on zotero.org — see Deliberate differences.
  • A deleted account breaks nothing. The block is simply left out.

items.title: Sorting by a person
items.text:
sort=addedBy orders by the author's displayed name. Where nobody is recorded — any personal library, and group items written before authorship was recorded — it sorts by dateAdded instead of failing.

The sort direction still follows the sort's name: anything starting with date defaults to descending, everything else to ascending. So sort=addedBy ascends even when it falls back to dateAdded, while sort=dateAdded descends. This is zotero.org's behavior.

sort=editedBy is altero's own. It has been requested from zotero.org since 2023 (dataserver#153) and not built. zotero.org answers Invalid 'sort' value to it; no client sends it today.

items.title: Pagination of the sync formats
items.text:
format=keys and format=versions have no page limit by default: they return everything in one response, with no Link header.

This matters. The desktop reads the whole of format=versions to decide what to sync. Cutting it to the usual 25 would not cause an error — the client would silently believe the library holds 25 objects. An explicit limit is still honored and is not capped at 100.

Every other format keeps a default of 25 and a maximum of 100.

items.title: Naming objects by key
items.text:
itemKey, collectionKey and searchKey behave alike:

  • Malformed keys are dropped, not refused. They could not have matched anything anyway.
  • The page size is always 100, whatever limit says. format=keys and format=versions are exempt and still answer with everything.
  • Each object type filters on its own parameter: collectionKey for collections, searchKey for saved searches.

All three matter because this is how a sync downloads changed objects: by key, in batches of 100. A library with fewer than 25 changes would hide any mistake here; one with hundreds would not.

items.title: Parameter handling
items.text: Behavior limit=0 or a negative limit falls back to the default rather than erroring A limit above the maximum is lowered to it, not refused sort=asc / sort=desc sets the direction and keeps the default sort qmode ignores case, so startsWith and startswith both work Sorts whose name begins with date default to descending; everything else to ascending itemType may not be repeated numItems is a valid sort only for tags extra and serverDateModified are valid item sorts

items.title: Response shapes
items.text:
These were confirmed against a live library.

  • A tag has no version of its own. Its envelope is {tag, links, meta}, with type and numItems in meta. Clients learn tag versions from format=versions.
  • meta leaves out what does not apply. creatorSummary is absent without creators, parsedDate without a date, and a child attachment's meta is {}. numChildren is always present. A summary reads Smith, Smith and Myers or Ranganathan et al.; parsedDate contains only the parts present, such as 2016 or 2018-05.
  • A write response shows each object as it was just written. A parent created in the same batch as its children reports the numChildren it had at that moment, as on zotero.org.
  • Error messages name the object: Item does not exist, Collection not found, Search not found, Invalid itemType 'bogus', Invalid 'sort' value 'bogus'.
  • An unreadable number is ignored. limit=abc answers 200 with the default page size. Only a value the server understands and disagrees with, such as an unknown sort, is a 400.
  • Links to the first page omit start=0: ?limit=2, not ?limit=2&start=0.
  • Field order decides whether an attachment can be saved. The desktop processes an attachment's fields in the order they arrive, and fails if filename comes before linkMode. The failure is not reported once: the item is retried and fails on every later sync. altero therefore always serves fields in the schema's order — for an attachment linkMode, title, accessDate, url, contentType, charset, filename, md5, mtime, note — which is also the order zotero.org uses.

items.title: Fields the published schema does not list
items.text:
The published schema gives attachments only title, accessDate and url, and notes and annotations no fields at all. In reality an attachment also has linkMode, contentType, charset, filename, md5, mtime and path; a note has note; and an annotation has the annotation* fields. Validating strictly against the published schema would even reject the server's own /items/new template, so altero accepts these fields too. Any other field outside the schema is still refused, so a storage field on a book is an error. md5 must be a 32-character digest, as zotero.org requires: the server serves the file a stored digest names, so a value that is not a digest is refused rather than allowed to name a file outside the store.

If a write is refused with Invalid field, this is the first thing to check.

md5 and mtime are null until a file has been uploaded, on attachments that store a file. A write that sends either as empty does not overwrite a stored value. The Android app depends on this: an empty string instead of null stopped it from ever uploading the file.

items.title: Timestamps
items.text: dateAdded and dateModified come from the client and are stored unchanged, so uploading an existing library keeps its history. serverDateModified is always the server's own time, so no client can reorder results by changing its own clock.

items.title: Citations and bibliographies
items.text:
Citation rendering runs locally with packaged CSL styles. No network fetch is needed during a request. CSL field mapping follows Zotero's schema.

Request Behavior format=csljson Wraps entries in {"items": [...]}, including a single item format=bib One document, at most 150 items; Total-Results but no pagination links format=bib with sorting or paging parameters 400 include outside JSON, an unknown include, or none combined with another 400 Unknown style name 404; renamed styles retain their aliases Style supplied as a URL 400; arbitrary remote styles are not fetched

include accepts data, bib, citation, csljson, none and supported export formats. Atom uses content for HTML. Titles and names escape markup except supported rich-text formatting such as italics, bold, superscript, subscript, small caps and nocase.

The server provides Zotero's bibliography export formats. API exports omit attachment bytes and child-note bundles; individual notes or attachments are handled as each format permits. BibTeX, BibLaTeX and RIS use CSL data, so some types become @misc or GEN. Citation keys use author, year and title with collision suffixes; an explicit citationKey takes precedence.

Deliberate output differences:

  • EndNote XML and Evernote identify altero as the writer.
  • XML and RDF preserve content without matching upstream whitespace.
  • CSV's Date Added contains the added date rather than the modified date.
  • Bookmarks and Evernote escape special characters correctly; Evernote dates have one trailing Z, and missing URLs are empty.
  • Multiple ISBNs do not create an extra empty RDF entry.
  • Duplicate TEI IDs receive suffixes as they are streamed.

Formatted citations preserve hanging indents and line spacing but do not reproduce numbered-style second-field-align. APA may repeat a title when an item lacks an author, a known processor limitation.

items.title: Item type schema
items.text:
These came from comparing all 163 schema responses with the live API.

  • /itemTypes and /itemFields are sorted by their translated names, so the order changes with locale. Sorting is by character code, so Software (computerProgram) sorts under S and TV Broadcast comes before Thesis.
  • /itemTypeCreatorTypes lists the primary creator type first, then the rest by translated name.
  • /itemFields leaves out base-only fields such as medium and authority. They are still accepted in writes.
  • Two templates disagree with the schema. For videoRecording and radioBroadcast the schema calls creator the primary creator type, yet /items/new fills those templates with director. altero reproduces both, so a template from altero is interchangeable with one from zotero.org.

items.title: The file protocol
items.text:
Uploading a file takes three requests — authorize, send the bytes, register — exactly as with zotero.org, including the uploadKey passed between them and the {"exists": 1} answer when the server already holds those bytes.

The middle step differs. zotero.org hands the client an Amazon S3 address plus a prefix and suffix to wrap around the file. altero points back at itself and leaves both empty, so the client sends the file as it is. A client that wraps the file as documented still sends exactly the file.

The mobile apps ask for a form. The iOS and Android apps add params=1 and then send the file as a form upload. altero answers that request shape too, with empty form fields, and accepts the file from a form or as a plain body.

Stale uploads are refused. Bytes are checked against the declared MD5 and length, and If-Match or If-None-Match is required, so a client working from outdated information cannot overwrite a newer file. A conflicting upload answers 412 with Last-Modified-Version set to the attachment's own version; the desktop uses that header to open its file-conflict dialog. Without it, two desktops racing to upload kept retrying instead of resolving the conflict.

A file is stored whole or not at all. An upload that stops part way — a full disk, a dropped network mount — leaves no file rather than a short one. That matters because files are stored by content: a damaged file would be reported as {"exists": 1} to every later client holding the same bytes, and each would mark its attachment as synced for good.

Registration therefore checks the stored file against its digest before attaching it. A file that is not what was sent is removed and the registration refused; the client treats that as a file-sync error and sends the file again on its next sync. Every stored file is named by the digest of its own bytes, so a mismatch is always damage.

An attachment can claim a file the server does not have. A library moved from zotero.org whose files were kept on WebDAV names a digest for every attachment, but none of the files. So If-None-Match: * ("is there a file to protect?") is answered by looking for the file itself, not at what the attachment claims; otherwise the upload that would repair the attachment is refused. If-Match is still checked against the attachment, because that is how the client proves it is not working from stale information.

A download serves the file an upload registered, not the one the attachment claims, as on zotero.org. md5 is metadata any client may write, and files are shared by digest across libraries, so serving the claim would hand anybody who knew a digest the file behind it. Writing md5 therefore changes what the attachment says and not which bytes it serves; an attachment no upload gave a file answers 404. A library copied from another, restored from an archive that carries the file, or upgraded from an earlier altero keeps the file it had.

{"exists": 1} needs the digest and the exact size, as on zotero.org: that answer gives the client the stored file without receiving a byte. The digest is the archive's, zipMD5, for a snapshot. Where the size differs, zotero.org refuses with 400; altero asks for the bytes instead, which then prove themselves, so a stored file that was damaged can be repaired by the next client that holds it.

No upload or restore can replace another library's file. A snapshot's md5 names the file inside the archive, and an archive's files/ entry names whatever its maker wrote there; neither is checked against the bytes. So the bytes are stored under their own digest, never under a name somebody gave them.

items.title: Downloading is a redirect, and has to be
items.text:
Asking for an attachment's file answers 302, with three headers:
