Header What it says Zotero-File-Modification-Time the modification time the uploading client declared Zotero-File-MD5 the attachment's file: for a snapshot, the one inside Zotero-File-Compressed Yes when the stored bytes are a ZIP around that file

The desktop reads these headers from the redirect and nowhere else. Answering 200 with the bytes makes every download fail with "A file sync error occurred". The redirect also lets the client skip the download entirely when the modification time shows its copy is current.

items.title: The location has to be a credential
items.text:
The desktop makes a new request to the redirect location without its API key. altero therefore issues a full URL at /storage/download/<key> that grants access to just that file for five minutes. It permits retries and forbids shared caching.

The URL never contains the account's long-lived API key. Callers that already hold a key can also fetch bytes directly at <prefix>/items/<key>/file/content.

items.title: Telling an archive from a file
items.text:
The desktop zips a web snapshot before uploading it. If a download then says Zotero-File-Compressed: No, the client saves the ZIP itself under the attachment's name, and the snapshot is quietly lost.

altero records which is which when the file is registered: an upload that came with a zipMD5 is an archive around the attachment's file, and a .docx or .epub — a ZIP itself — uploaded without one is served as it is. An archive restored into a library is one when its own digest is not the name the archive filed it under and it starts like a ZIP, which is how earlier altero versions stored snapshots.

items.title: Obtaining a key
items.text:
The desktop creates a login session with POST /keys/sessions, opens its loginURL, and polls until approved. A completed response includes apiKey, userID, username, displayName and emails.

Approval in altero requires fresh identity confirmation before issuing a long-lived key. The key includes group access so the client does not mistake unreadable groups for lost libraries. Shell approval remains available when the browser interface is not built.

A profile requesting one account number cannot be approved for another: the client would offer to reset its data directory. Changing the username alone is safe because the client identifies the account by number.

Usernames cannot contain @; sign-in distinguishes usernames from email addresses by that character. An account has at most one email address and reports it only after confirmation. loginURL always has a query so mobile clients can append &app=1.

Legacy password-to-key POST /keys is unsupported. Key management is available in Settings and the CLI, rather than through /users/<id>/keys. A key may read /keys/current and revoke itself.

items.title: A credential that gave up notes or files
items.text:
A credential says four things about a library: whether it may read it, write to it, read its notes, and download its files. An API key carries them as library, write, notes and files; an OAuth token as the scopes library.read, library.write, notes.read and files.read. Notes and files only ever narrow reading: without read access there are no notes or files either.

A hidden note is hidden completely. Without note access, a note answers 404 by key and is missing from every listing, export, key list and version list. numChildren does not count it, and a tag carried only by hidden notes disappears from item-scoped tag lists. This is what zotero.org does. Serving the note with its text blanked would tell the caller it exists.

Without file access, only the bytes are refused. The download endpoints answer 403, but the attachment itself — with its md5, filename and contentType — is still served.

Two rules from zotero.org that are not guessable:

  • An anonymous reader of a public library can read its notes but not its files. In a public group, only members have file access.
  • A credential never sees less of a public library than a visitor with no credential at all. Notes in a public library are readable whatever the credential says. Files are not, for the reason above.

File access does not cover the full text. A credential that may read the library may read an attachment's extracted text, even without file access — as on zotero.org. The consent screen's Download your attachments is about the files themselves.

Two deliberate differences:

  • The restrictions apply to group libraries too. zotero.org applies them only to the personal library. A consent screen that says Read your notes should mean it everywhere.
  • Uploading depends on write access, not on file access. At zotero.org one files permission covers both directions. Here it is named for downloading, and the consent screen says Download your attachments, so it does not also grant uploads. Write access and the group's file-editing setting decide who may upload.

None of this changes what the desktop sees: the keys it receives, and every key made in the browser or on the command line, carry all four permissions. Only an OAuth token can lack them.

items.title: What the desktop client actually sends
items.text:
The desktop relies on behavior beyond the published request examples:

  • mtime is a numeric millisecond timestamp and requires 64-bit storage.
  • Full text is uploaded as a POST <prefix>/fulltext batch with If-Unmodified-Since-Version. Result entries are objects containing key.
  • Recreating a setting clears its deletion record, so deletion processing does not erase the new value.
  • A bare DELETE <prefix>/tags answers 204 without deleting anything. The client can drop the query naming the tags; it accepts only 204 or 412. An explicit tags=a||b is also supported.
  • Gzipped bodies are accepted. Compressed and expanded bodies are each limited to 128 MiB; invalid compression returns 400 and excess size returns 413.
  • Snapshots carry md5 for the main file and zipMD5 for the archive. Transfer validation uses the archive digest.
  • Upload addresses must be absolute URLs.
  • Batch uploads contain partial changes after the first sync; see patch semantics.
  • File registration advances the library version. A following stale full-text upload can receive 412 and retry after syncing.

A client's version ahead of the server is accepted, as upstream. The desktop then refuses a lower response version. Raising the server counter resolves that mismatch but recreates no data; follow the recovery procedure.

Retraction-list requests return 404 because altero has no retraction data. The client logs the error and continues syncing.

The streaming URL is independent of the API URL. Configure both, or disable streaming explicitly, to avoid sending the altero key to Zotero's default streaming service. See client setup.

items.title: The streaming API
items.text:
Served at /stream, not on a separate host, and the client is pointed at it with extensions.zotero.streaming.url. It follows the published protocol. Both ways of subscribing work: an API key in the handshake, and createSubscriptions naming a key and no topics, which is what the desktop sends.

Three topics that are not libraries are accepted, because the client asks for them on every connection:

  • styles and translators are accepted but never fire; the client updates those on its own schedule.
  • login-session:<token> tells the client the moment a login is approved, instead of at its next poll. It needs the session's token, and on approval it carries the same body the poll returns. An approval from altero login approve on the command line is not announced; the client's poll finishes the login as before.

Removing a subscription that does not exist is ignored, instead of closing with 4409. The client's login flow does exactly that, and treats an unexpected close as its own error and stops reconnecting.

subscriptionsDeleted names what was removed, which the client needs.

Guessed rather than copied, since there is no reference implementation:

  • Close code 4400 for a message that is not JSON or asks for something unknown, continuing the documented 4403, 4409 and 4413.
  • At most 50 subscriptions per connection. The documentation says a limit exists but not what it is; the desktop holds one.
  • topicAdded and topicRemoved go only to subscriptions that named no topics. A client that chose its topics is not given new ones.

An event is sent only once its write is committed. A client told about a version that was then rolled back would ask for it and find the library older — indistinguishable from a server that went backwards.

One process only. Events are passed around in memory. With several worker processes, a client hears only about writes handled by its own worker; the others fall back on polling, as before.

items.title: Atom
items.text:
format=atom is served for items, collections, saved searches and tags, both for lists and single objects. content chooses what goes inside: html by default, or json, bib, citation, csljson, an export format, none, or several at once. The shapes were copied from zotero.org.

Five differences, most following from decisions elsewhere on this page:

  • No rel="alternate" links. See Deliberate differences.
  • <id> uses the address the request came to, not zotero.org.
  • Feed titles start with altero, not Zotero. The rest of the wording is zotero.org's.
  • No rel="first" link on the first page. The feed's links and the Link header come from one place, so they cannot disagree.
  • The HTML table lists fields in the item's own order. zotero.org orders them by an internal number the published schema does not include.

A <content> element carries both zapi:type and a media type, so readers looking for either find it. A bibliography that is not valid XML is escaped and marked as HTML, so one bad entry cannot make the whole feed unreadable.

content is refused outside format=atom, and a citation is refused for collections, saved searches and tags: an empty answer would look the same as an object without one.

items.title: API versions
items.text: Only version 3 is served. Asking for another version, by the Zotero-API-Version header or the v parameter, is a 400: older clients expect different envelopes, parameter names and pagination, and version 3 answers under an older label would be worse than a refusal. A header and a parameter that disagree are refused too, as on zotero.org.

items.title: The relations map
items.text:
A relation with one target is a string; with several it becomes an array. Zotero relies on this — an item related to three others names all three under dc:relation — so the shape matters.

Collections carry relations too, and they are stored like items' relations.

An empty array is accepted in place of an empty object, as zotero.org allows.

Not copied: zotero.org accepts only certain relation types and requires Zotero addresses as values. altero accepts any. That is the permissive direction, so no client breaks, but a library moved from altero to zotero.org could carry a relation zotero.org refuses.

items.title: Backoff and Retry-After
items.text:
The desktop ignores both headers unless they are whole seconds, and 0 is as useless as a fraction. Without Retry-After, a 429 still works, but the client has to guess how long to wait.

altero answers 429 with a whole-second Retry-After of at least 1. It does not send Backoff, which asks clients to slow down while still being served; that needs a measure of load altero does not have.

On SQLite, a write that waits more than five seconds for another write to finish answers 503 with Retry-After: 5. Nothing has been written at that point. The desktop retries such a 503 and would report any other server error as a sync error. PostgreSQL waits instead and never gives this answer.

items.title: My Publications
items.text:
/users/<id>/publications/items can be read without a key, as on zotero.org. Only items marked inPublications appear, in items, items/top and by key; any other key answers 404, so an item hidden from the list cannot be fetched directly either.

publications/collections and publications/searches answer 404, as on zotero.org. Nothing can be written here: an item joins the list by being saved in the library with inPublications set.

There is no group version. My Publications belongs to a person, which is also why inPublications is refused on a group item.

publications/settings and publications/deleted are served and always empty, because the client polls both and treats anything but 200 as a failed sync.

An obsolete upstream publications guard returned 400 for some libraries. altero does not reproduce that legacy refusal, which would break current clients.

items.title: Who may read My Publications
items.text:
At zotero.org anybody can. altero keeps that as the default and lets each account narrow it, because a personal server is not a public service — see Sharing. The setting applies to the API as well as to the profile page:

Setting No key Any key from this server A key that may read the library public (default) 200 200 200 users 403 200 200 private 403 403 200

The last column is why the owner's desktop keeps syncing: its key may read the library, so closing the page never breaks the sync that fills it. Every publications endpoint applies the setting, including the settings and deleted polls. An instance that never changes the setting behaves exactly like zotero.org.

items.title: Profile pages
items.text:
zotero.org's profile page is zotero.org/<name>, with the username simplified for the address. altero serves the same page at /app/u/<username>. The prefix keeps a username such as settings from colliding with the interface's own pages. Both the username and zotero.org's simplified form work, in any letter case.

The heading shows the real name, or the username when there is none. There is no link to zotero.org, for the same reason as everywhere else.

items.title: Publishing from the browser
items.text:
The API knows only the inPublications flag, but publishing is more than that. Before setting it, the desktop asks four questions: whether files go along, whether notes go along, whether an existing Rights value stays, and which license the work is published under. altero's browser interface asks the same four and follows the desktop's rules:

Rule Child notes go along only when chosen Stored files go along only when chosen Links to web pages always go along Linked files never do, because the server does not hold them Annotations never do The license is written into Rights unless an existing value was chosen to stay Removing an item takes its notes and attachments with it, including trashed ones Removing something that is not published is an error

These requests belong to the browser interface and cannot be made with an API key.

Three deliberate differences:

  • The license name is written in English, whatever language the account uses. The desktop writes the name in the language of its own window, so the same license reaches the field in German from one client and in English from another. Rights is data that gets exported and cited, not a label, so it should not depend on who published.
  • The license chooser remains available afterwards. The desktop never shows its wizard twice for an item; a different license is typed into the Rights field. The browser offers a chooser with the same licenses and free text. It refuses the edit if Rights changed in the meantime; changes to other fields do not prevent saving.
  • The generic "Creative Commons" choice is not offered. It is what the desktop reports while a license is still being chosen; here, choosing Creative Commons always leads on to the two questions that pick one of the six licenses.

items.title: Trashing a collection or a saved search
items.text:
Zotero trashes collections and saved searches by marking them deleted, and syncs that mark like any other property.

Trashed collections and searches stay in the listings, marked deleted: 1, because the client has no way to ask for trashed ones separately. Hiding them would tell the client they were gone, not trashed.

Their counts follow zotero.org, and differ: numCollections includes trashed subcollections, numItems leaves out trashed items.

Items are unaffected: they have their own trash endpoint, and /items still leaves trashed ones out.

The value must be true, false, 0 or 1; otherwise the string "false" would count as trashed.

items.title: inPublications
items.text:
An ordinary item property. Setting it to true is refused in three cases:

Refused Message A group library Group items cannot be added to My Publications A top-level note or attachment Top-level notes and attachments cannot be added to My Publications A linked-file attachment Linked-file attachments cannot be added to My Publications

Child notes and attachments are allowed; that is what My Publications is for. A linked file is not, because the server does not hold the file.

The property appears only when true, as deleted does.

A partial write that leaves it out leaves it alone, and the same goes for deleted. So changing an item's title does not take it out of the trash or out of My Publications. A PUT still clears what it leaves out; the client always sends deleted: false explicitly when restoring.

Reading the public list is described under My Publications; publishing with the desktop wizard's options, under Publishing from the browser.

items.title: A POSTed batch is a batch of patches
items.text:
In a POST to /items, /collections or /searches:

  • an entry naming an object that exists may leave out anything it is not changing, and what it leaves out stays as it was;
  • an entry for a new object must still contain what a new object needs: a collection its name, a saved search its conditions, an item its type.

PUT replaces the whole object: what it leaves out is cleared.

An entry with a version above 0 must name an existing object. If the object is gone, that entry fails with 404, even if it is complete. The desktop needs the 404 to settle an edit made against an object deleted elsewhere; recreating the object silently would undo the deletion. New objects use version 0 or no version.

This is the desktop's normal way of uploading: it remembers the last synced copy of each object and sends only the difference. Two common cases:

The user did What the client uploads Sent a collection to the trash {key, version, deleted: true} Changed an item's type {key, version, itemType}

Treated as complete objects, the first would be refused for lacking a name — stopping the whole library's sync — and the second would wipe every field, creator, tag and collection it did not mention.

Leaving a property out means "unchanged"; sending it empty clears it. That matters for the four list properties: creators, tags, collections and relations. The desktop really sends collections: [] to take an item out of its last collection — for example after saving into a collection with the browser connector and then switching the save target to the library root. Treating empty as absent would leave the item filed, and the client would upload the same change on every sync forever.

Regular-item sync responses include empty creators, tags, collections and relations; see Empty creators.

Changing an item's type keeps what the new type can hold. A field the new type lacks moves to its equivalent there, as a book's publisher becomes a report's institution, or is cleared. A creator whose role the new type lacks becomes a contributor. A field sent empty is accepted even if the new type lacks it, because that is how the desktop clears one: it uploads {key, version, itemType} with every field the item lost set to "". Fields and creators sent with the type are taken as sent.

parentItem: false makes a child top-level. The desktop sends it when a note or attachment is moved out to the library. As on zotero.org, a patch that files a child in a collection without mentioning parentItem does the same, since a child cannot be in a collection.

items.title: Objects that were sent again without changing
items.text:
An object identical to the stored one is reported as unchanged and keeps its version, as on zotero.org. Saving it again would advance the library version and make every other client download an object that never changed.

Everything a client can set counts as a change: type, fields, creators and their order, relations, parent, trash flag, dateAdded, dateModified, tags and collections. The server's own values — the version and serverDateModified — do not. Leaving dateModified out is no change by itself: the server stamps it only when something else changed. A batch in which nothing changed leaves the library version as it was.

Settings follow the same rule: a setting is changed only if its value differs, so 3 and 3.0 differ but 3 and 3 do not. A request that changes no setting answers 204 with the library version unchanged; in a batch, only the settings that changed get the new version.

The current dataserver advances the library version for each object in a batch, even an unchanged one. altero advances it once per request that changes something. Object versions and the reported results still agree; only the library's version number can differ between the two servers.

Two places skip this check, as on zotero.org: a single-object PUT or PATCH, which has no report to put the answer in, and the full-text batch.

items.title: An object that depends on one the server lacks
items.text:
An item naming a parent item or a collection that does not exist, or a collection naming a parent collection that does not exist, fails with 409, as on zotero.org. In a batch, the failure names the missing object in data:

Missing message data Parent item Parent item K not found {"parentItem": "K"} Collection Collection K not found {"collection": "K"} Parent collection Parent collection K not found {"collection": "K"}

The desktop reads data to repair its own state: if it holds the missing object but has not queued it, it marks it for upload and syncs again. Without data, the same item fails on every sync.

An object outside what the credential may read is reported as missing in the same way, so a write cannot be used to learn whether a key exists.

items.title: What may be a child of what
items.text:
The rules are zotero.org's, and the desktop applies the same ones before it uploads:

Item May hang off Regular item nothing Note a regular item Attachment a regular item; an embedded image (a picture in a note) also a note Annotation a file attachment, required: a highlight, underline or note annotation on a PDF, EPUB or HTML snapshot; an image, ink or text annotation on a PDF

A note or attachment under a note or attachment fails with 409, Parent item cannot be a note or attachment, naming the parent in data. The other refusals fail with 400, including an item named as its own parent.

The rules are checked when an item is created or moved to another parent. An item already stored under a parent it could not have now, for example by an earlier altero, keeps syncing as it is.

Child items cannot belong to collections. Making a standalone note or attachment a child removes its former collection memberships, even when the upload omits collections. Explicitly assigning a child to a collection fails with 400, as on zotero.org.

items.title: Groups
items.text:
zotero.org has endpoints for creating, editing and deleting groups and adding members, but only for its own administrators, in XML, and never used by the Zotero client. An ordinary key gets 403.

altero serves the same paths for ordinary users, with an API key and JSON in the shape GET /groups/<id> already returns, so what was read can be sent back. Inventing a separate administrator credential would have meant a second kind of credential on a server whose permissions are otherwise per library.

PUT replaces and PATCH updates, as for items. A PUT without a type makes the group private, the safe default. POST /groups/<id>/users adds a member by userID or username.

To You need Create a group a key that may write to your own library Read one membership, or a public group Write items to one membership, plus the group's editing setting Upload files to one membership, plus the group's file setting Change its details, add or remove members to be an administrator of the group Leave nothing but your own decision Hand it over, delete it to be its owner

Two of these are altero's own rules. A key must be allowed to write to the group and its owner must administer it, because adding items and deciding who else may are different things. Only the owner can hand over or delete a group, because both end it as its members know it.

A key's "all groups" means the groups its owner belongs to, never every group on the server.

Changing a group's details or its members advances the library's version. zotero.org keeps a separate group version; altero reports the library's for both. A role change therefore costs connected clients one sync that finds nothing new — the cheaper mistake, since a client that has not noticed a demotion still believes it may write.

items.title: Group renames notify connected clients
items.text: A group rename advances its advertised version and sends a committed topicUpdated event, so clients refresh their cached group name. Item versions need not change. Upstream's missing-notification report is unverified against the hosted service; altero deliberately keeps this behavior (dataserver#92).

items.title: Who the client finds in a group
items.text:
Group listings always carry a Link header, even when empty or a single page. The desktop's account settings read it unconditionally and fail without it. zotero.org always includes an alternate link to itself; altero includes self instead. A page holds 25 groups by default; format=versions is unlimited.

A group's JSON lists admins and members as user ids, and the desktop needs them: it makes a group library editable for the owner, for administrators, and for members when the group lets members edit. Anyone found in neither list syncs the library read-only. The owner is in neither list, as on zotero.org, and empty lists are left out. The lists are read-only; membership has its own endpoints.

Only members see the lists. zotero.org shows them to anyone who can read the group, which for a public group is anybody. Nobody outside a group syncs it, so for a stranger the lists would only reveal who belongs.

The client fetches a group again only when its version changes, so every membership change advances it — from the API, the browser, the command line or an accepted invitation.

items.title: Finer roles for one member
items.text:
A Zotero group decides who may edit for the whole group at once: members or only administrators. Read-only members, members who may add but not remove, and members who may change only their own items have been requested on the Zotero forums since 2010 (discussion 14053). altero has all three, as a permission per member, alongside their role.

A role says whether somebody helps run the group; a permission says how far they may go with its contents. An administrator can be an ordinary contributor, and a member can be limited to reading, without changing anybody's role.

Permission Creates Changes Removes Collections and searches inherit ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ read add ✓ anything make and change, never remove own ✓ its own its own read-only

Four decisions shape it:

  • It only ever restricts. It is applied last, after the key's permissions, membership and the group's own editing setting. A member marked add in a group where only administrators edit still cannot edit.
  • Moving to the trash counts as removing, because that is how the desktop deletes. Otherwise a member who may not delete could still empty the library. Restoring from the trash is allowed.
  • The shared structure belongs to nobody. Nothing records who made a collection, saved search or setting, so own treats all of them as somebody else's. Filing your own item into a collection is a change to the item and is allowed: contributors put their work where the group's structure says, but cannot restructure it.
  • Administrators cannot be restricted. They can edit any membership, including their own, so a restriction would be shown but not enforced. Making somebody an administrator clears theirs.

items.title: One library version, two representations
items.text:
read is the only permission Zotero clients already understand: a read-only member is told the group's editing setting is "administrators only", while everybody else sees the real setting. The client then shows the library read-only, as it does for any member of such a group.

So the same library version looks different to different people. That is sound, because a group never had one view for everyone — a stranger gets 404 where a member gets 200 — and a member's view changes only when the library's version does, which changing a permission causes.

items.title: add and own surface as sync errors
items.text:
Zotero clients have no way to show these two, and altero does not invent one. A restricted member's desktop shows the library as editable, and a forbidden write comes back as 403 with an explanation:

  • You can add to this group library but not remove from it
  • You can only change what you added to this group library
  • You can only remove what you added to this group library

The desktop shows this as a sync error, and the sentence is the only explanation the member gets. Anyone setting add or own should know that is how it looks from the other side. The browser interface knows both permissions and hides what they forbid.

items.title: Where a permission is set
items.text: In the browser on the group's member list; in an invitation, so that "come and read this" and "come and help" are different invitations; with altero group permission <group> <username> <permission>; or through the API with PUT /groups/<id>/users/<userID>, which takes permission alongside role. When both are sent, the role is applied first, so a demotion followed by a restriction ends with the restriction.

items.title: Renaming a tag
items.text:
PATCH <prefix>/tags/<name> with {"tag": "<new name>"} renames a tag and answers 204 with the new Last-Modified-Version.

zotero.org has no such endpoint: renaming is left to the client, item by item, and has been requested since 2016 (dataserver#108). So the endpoint is altero's own, and its behavior is copied from the desktop's own rename:

  • Both kinds of tag are renamed. A name can belong to a manual tag and an automatic one at the same time; both are renamed, just as deleting a tag deletes both.
  • Exactly one tag is left under the new name, carrying every item that had either name — including an automatic tag that already had the new name.
  • The renamed tag is manual. Renaming is how an automatic tag stops being one, in the desktop too.
  • Items already carrying the new name are left alone, and an item that carried both names ends up with it once.
  • Every affected item gets the new library version, so other clients download it. Their dateModified stays as it was, because no client made that change.
  • The old name is recorded as deleted, as if it had been deleted, and any deletion record for the new name is cleared. Otherwise one sync could tell a client both "remove this tag" and "here are items with it".

If-Unmodified-Since-Version is required. Renaming a tag to its own name changes nothing and does not advance the library version. An unknown tag is a 404; an empty name, or one longer than 255 characters, is a 400.

The browser uses the same operation; see Tags.

items.title: The desktop client's three extra views
items.text:
These views exist only in the browser. Zotero computes them from its local library; its API has no corresponding scopes.

View altero behavior Unfiled Items Untrashed top-level items in no collection Duplicate Items Shared normalized DOI/ISBN, or normalized title plus matching surname or year; title alone only when neither has creators or year Recently Read Items with attachments read within 90 days, and standalone attachments read in that period

Duplicate detection compares regular items across types. It suggests candidates, not proof that they are the same work. The 90-day reading window is an explicit guess; the desktop's exact rule is undocumented.

There is no v3 /items/unfiled. Unknown query parameters are ignored, so scope=unfiled or unfiled=1 on a v3 item listing does not filter it.

items.title: Merging PDFs with embedded notes
items.text:
When deduplication would both move a surviving PDF to the master and transfer another PDF's embedded note to it, altero keeps both PDFs under the master. Each keeps its original note and annotations. Other PDF matching follows the desktop's byte and common-word checks.

A recorded desktop defect can save the note while losing the parent change. Keeping both files avoids leaving the survivor under a trashed duplicate. See the historical desktop evidence.

items.title: Reading a library out of zotero.org
items.text:
The migration reads a personal library from api.zotero.org and turns it into the same archive altero library export writes, then restores that archive. It makes no writes to zotero.org.

It needs an API key. zotero.org offers no password sign-in for software, and OAuth would require every altero instance to register with Zotero. The key is used for the import and then forgotten.

Three things zotero.org's API does not provide, and what altero uses instead:

Missing Instead serverDateModified The item's dateModified, which is the same moment for anything a client last wrote Dates for collections, saved searches and tags The time of the import Versions of deleted objects The library's current version, so a client asking what was deleted since any earlier point hears about all of it

Links between items are rewritten to the new account. Related items, merge records and similar links name the account they belong to as http://zotero.org/users/<id>/items/<key>. The account number is changed to the new one, or every link would point to an account this server does not know. The zotero.org part stays, because the desktop recognizes these links only in that exact form. Links into group libraries are left as they are, since groups are not imported.

zotero.org's rate limits are obeyed the way the desktop obeys altero's: requests go one at a time, Backoff pauses before the next request, and a 429 waits as long as Retry-After says — or, without it, a doubling delay starting at one second.

/tags?format=versions fails on api.zotero.org with a server error, for every library tried, including Zotero's own example account. A real import stopped on it after reading everything else. So the import treats only items, collections and saved searches as essential and stops if one cannot be read. Tag versions, settings, full text, the deletion log and attachment files are read if possible and listed in the report if not. A tag without a version gets the library's, which is the safe direction: clients asking what changed hear about it.

Pages are fetched by position, not by following the Link header, because that header always points at api.zotero.org.

items.title: Continuous sync with zotero.org
items.text:
Continuous two-way sync is unsupported and is not feasible as a transparent mode for unmodified Zotero Desktop. Each server assigns library and object versions independently. After a migration, version 100 on altero and version 100 on zotero.org can describe different changes. The desktop remembers one server's watermark and cached object versions; changing the API address does not reconcile those histories. Keeping the same account number and item keys does not solve that problem.

A separate replication service would need its own per-server version history, conflict resolution, deletion tracking, relation mapping and attachment transfer. Copying objects and their version numbers back and forth is not such a service. altero does not provide one, and alternating a desktop between servers is not a supported way to keep them synchronized.

A periodic one-way refresh from zotero.org into altero is feasible as future work, with zotero.org authoritative and the destination treated as a copy. It would need to apply upstream changes and deletions through altero's own versioned writes so already-connected clients can observe them. Local edits would need an explicit refusal or overwrite policy. This is a design assessment, not an implemented or tested refresh feature; scheduling and its implementation remain future work.

Today, the CLI and browser offer a one-time personal-library import. Repeating it with --replace restores a whole snapshot and can discard altero-only changes. It does not perform incremental reconciliation, and raising the library watermark alone cannot replace newer objects already cached by a desktop with older imported versions. See the exercised recovery limits. Use the migration procedure to move to altero, then keep that library's clients pointed at altero.

items.title: Token revocation
items.text: /oauth/revoke accepts the same client authentication methods as /oauth/token: HTTP Basic, a form secret, or a public client's ID without a secret. Confidential clients must authenticate, as RFC 7009 §2.1 requires. An authenticated request gets 200 for an unknown token too, and cannot revoke another client's token. Revoking an access token leaves its refresh token usable; revoking a refresh token invalidates its whole family.

items.title: A second credential for the v3 API
items.text:
The v3 API is authenticated by a credential sent with each request, never by a browser cookie. The authorization server lets an OAuth access token be that credential, alongside an API key; the rule itself is unchanged.

That distinction is the whole reason it is allowed. A browser attaches cookies to requests any website can trigger, so a cookie that worked on /users/<id>/items would expose the entire sync protocol to cross-site attacks. A token is sent only by the application holding it, and no other website can make it be sent.

/keys/current and /keys/<key> refuse access tokens. They describe and revoke an API key; a token is not one.

items.title: Confining a grant to particular resources
items.text:
A scope says what an application may do, never where. library.read means the whole personal library and groups.read every group the account belongs to — usually more than an application needs. On the consent screen the account holder can therefore narrow a grant to particular libraries, or to particular collections in them: "group 42 and none of my others", "the Reading collection and nothing else".

zotero.org has nothing like this, so there is nothing to copy, and API keys are unaffected. Grants made before this feature existed stay unrestricted.

A collection means the branch: everything nested inside it, at any depth, and anything filed there later — as with shared links and the desktop's Show Items from Subcollections. Otherwise filing a paper into a subcollection would quietly withdraw it from the application. Granting a subcollection does not grant its parent.

What a collection grant reaches: items filed in the granted collections, plus their notes, attachments and annotations — child items are never filed in collections themselves, and a paper without its PDF would be useless. Nothing else: an unfiled item is outside, and so is an item filed only elsewhere, with its children.

Refusals reveal nothing. A collection outside the grant is absent from every listing and answers 404 by key, and so does an item inside one — directly, through its children, its file, its full text, or a write naming it. 404, not 403, so an application cannot map the parts it was kept out of by guessing keys. A whole library that was not granted answers 403, since the caller already named it. Renaming tags, deleting saved searches and deleting settings answer the same way, so they cannot be used to probe for names either.

My Publications keeps its notes. Published items can be read with no credential at all, so a confined token still sees their notes — but only the published items inside its grant, which is less than an anonymous visitor sees and the right way round.

Four things a confined grant never gets, because they belong to no collection:

  • Saved searches. A saved search reaches wherever its conditions reach. /searches answers with an empty list.
  • Settings, such as tag colors. /settings answers with an empty object.
  • The deletion log. A deleted object no longer says which collections it was in, so there is no way to tell whether it was inside the grant. /deleted reports nothing.
  • Changing the library's structure: no creating, renaming or deleting collections, no saved searches, no settings, no tag renames (a rename changes items outside the grant too), and no group changes or new groups. Items inside the grant stay writable if the scopes allow it.

An item can be moved between granted collections but not out of them, and a new item must be placed in a granted collection.

GET /users/<id>/groups lists only granted groups, and the groups claim in user info and ID tokens is narrowed the same way.

The restriction belongs to the grant, not to a token, so a refreshed token keeps it; otherwise an application could simply wait for it to expire. Deleting the last collection a grant named leaves it reaching less, never everything.

items.title: Signing ID tokens while still not verifying them
items.text: As a client, altero accepts an ID token delivered directly by a trusted provider over TLS under the conditions below. As a provider, it signs its own ID tokens with RS256 and verifies its own signatures during logout, using only its stored keys and fixed algorithm.

items.title: No dynamic client registration
items.text: Applications must be registered by an operator. Redirect addresses and allowed scopes are reviewed at registration; no dynamic registration endpoint is provided.

items.title: PKCE is required, and S256 is the only method
items.text: The plain method makes the challenge identical to the secret it protects, so anyone who intercepts the code has everything needed to use it. altero neither offers nor accepts it, and requires PKCE from every application, including those with a client secret.

items.title: Scopes are refused rather than narrowed
items.text:
An unknown scope, a scope the application is not registered for, or one useless without another is an error, rather than being quietly dropped. Dropping it would produce an application that half works and a person who cannot tell which half. library.write without library.read is the useless case.

There is no annotations.* scope: annotations are items, and the API has no separate permission for them.

items.title: Not verifying the ID token's signature
items.text:
altero does not verify signatures on ID tokens received from an external provider. OpenID Connect Core §3.1.3.7 item 6 permits reliance on TLS for a token received directly from the token endpoint in this flow.

This requires altero to be a confidential client using authorization code and PKCE, and to receive the token from the provider rather than the browser. Issuer, audience, authorized party, nonce, expiry, issue time and subject are still validated. Supporting public clients would require revisiting this choice.

items.title: Reading a SAML assertion out of what was signed
items.text:
Only claims inside the verified signed portion of a SAML document are read. Signature verification is delegated to the XML-signature library. Altero also checks success status, validity, audience, recipient, request correlation and single use; a signature alone does not establish these.

Supported sign-in starts at altero and uses signed, unencrypted assertions. Unsolicited assertions, encryption and SAML Single Logout are unsupported.

items.title: Finishing SAML account linking with the browser session
items.text:
A cross-site assertion POST lacks the existing browser session cookie. For account linking and identity confirmation, altero verifies the assertion then redirects through a short-lived GET handoff that can recover that session.

The same signed-in account must finish it within two minutes. Handles are single-use, stored in the database for worker independence, and grant no access without the matching session. Ordinary sign-in can create its session directly. No browser cookie acquires Zotero API access.

items.title: Deliberate differences
items.text:
Seven places where altero does not copy zotero.org:

  • No alternate links. zotero.org links every object to its page on zotero.org. altero will not send clients to somebody else's copy of the data, and its own interface has no page per object, so envelopes carry only self and up. A single-page response therefore has no Link header — except group listings, which carry self because the desktop needs the header (see Who the client finds in a group).
  • An unknown locale falls back to en-US. zotero.org answers 500.
  • A regular item given a parent fails with 400. zotero.org answers 500 for the same refusal.
  • Rate limiting is off unless configured. A self-hosted server with a handful of clients rarely needs it; set ALTERO_RATE_LIMIT to turn it on.
  • Fields with the same translated name may be ordered differently. Three fields are called "Format"; zotero.org orders them by an internal number the published schema lacks.
  • Tags can be renamed through the API — see Renaming a tag. An addition rather than a change: nothing that reads tags behaves differently.
  • Library migration reads zotero.org without writing back — see import and continuous-sync limits.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: Use this reference to look up a setting and its default. For a new server, start with Deployment.

items.title: Where a setting comes from
items.text:
Three sources, in increasing order of precedence:

  1. the built-in defaults listed below
  2. config.py, a Python module of uppercase names
  3. ALTERO_-prefixed environment variables

The name is the same in both places: PUBLIC_URL in config.py is ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL in the environment. The tables below give the environment form, because that is what a container takes.

A misspelled name in config.py stops the server with Unknown setting. A misspelled environment variable is ignored, the environment being a namespace altero does not own.

items.title: From a source checkout
items.text:
Copy the example and edit it:

cp config.example.py config.py

config.py is ignored by git, so local settings stay out of the repository. Point ALTERO_CONFIG at another path to load a configuration module from somewhere else.

For a one-off change, set the variable on the command line instead:

ALTERO_PORT=9000 ALTERO_DEBUG=true uv run altero

items.title: In Docker
items.text:
Put .env beside your Compose file: docker/.env for the repository layout, or .env beside a downloaded compose.yaml. Every ALTERO_ setting in it reaches the container:

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=a-real-password
ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL=https://zotero.example.org
ALTERO_SMTP_URL=smtp://mail.example.org:587
ALTERO_MAIL_FROM=zotero@example.org
ALTERO_OPEN_REGISTRATION=true
ALTERO_RATE_LIMIT=600

The file is handed to the container whole, so keep out of it anything the application should not hold. ALTERO_IMAGE_TAG and ALTERO_PUBLISH_PORT belong there too, though they are read by Compose rather than by altero.

No .env is needed at all: an instance running on the defaults never writes one.

A variable exported in the shell wins over the file for ALTERO_SMTP_URL, ALTERO_MAIL_FROM, ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL and ALTERO_SSO_ONLY, which compose.yaml names itself. ALTERO_DATABASE_URL is always the stack's own database; point altero at an external one with a second Compose file rather than with .env:

# docker/compose.settings.yaml
services:
  altero:
    environment:
      ALTERO_DATABASE_URL: postgresql+asyncpg://user:password@db.example.org:5432/altero

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml -f docker/compose.settings.yaml up -d

docker compose ... config prints the merged result, which is how to see what the container will actually be given:

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml config

The image sets ALTERO_STORAGE_PATH=/data/storage, ALTERO_HOST=0.0.0.0 and ALTERO_PORT=8000 itself. /data is the volume, so leave the storage path alone unless you also move the mount.

Without ALTERO_DATABASE_URL, as when the image runs on its own, the database is SQLite at /data/altero.sqlite. That default comes from the image's own /app/config.py. A config.py mounted there replaces it.

items.title: Values
items.text: Booleans accept true, 1, yes and on, and their opposites, in any case. Durations are whole seconds, hours or days as the name says. An empty string is a real value and usually means "off" or "fall back": ALTERO_SMTP_URL= writes mail to the log.

items.title: Server and storage
items.text: Setting Default What it does ALTERO_DATABASE_URL sqlite+aiosqlite:///altero.sqlite SQLAlchemy URL. The driver must be an async one: sqlite+aiosqlite or postgresql+asyncpg. ALTERO_DATABASE_POOL_SIZE 5 Database connections kept open for requests to share. ALTERO_DATABASE_MAX_OVERFLOW 10 Further connections opened when the pool is exhausted. A request waiting longer than 30 s for one fails. ALTERO_HOST 127.0.0.1 Interface to bind. The container sets 0.0.0.0. ALTERO_PORT 8000 Port to bind, 1–65535. ALTERO_STORAGE_PATH ./storage Directory holding attachment files. The container sets /data/storage. ALTERO_MAX_UPLOAD_MB 1024 Largest attachment file accepted, in MiB, from a sync client or the browser. Larger uploads get 413. ALTERO_DEBUG false Debug behavior, SQL echoing and auto-reload. Never enable in production.

items.title: Accounts
items.text: Setting Default What it does ALTERO_OPEN_REGISTRATION false Whether anybody may register from the browser. First-account and invited-address registration are also available, except in SSO-only mode. ALTERO_PASSWORD_RESET false Offer self-service password reset for confirmed addresses. Requires SMTP and a public URL. Administrators can issue reset links independently, except in SSO-only mode. ALTERO_SSO_ONLY false Require configured OIDC/SAML providers for browser authentication and recent SSO proof for sensitive actions. Disables local credentials, registration, recovery, email changes and MFA; requires ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL. See SSO-only mode.

items.title: Public URL and email
items.text: Setting Default What it does ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL (empty) The stable external URL for API object links, file transfers and email links. Required for SMTP, single sign-on, passkeys and the authorization server. See Public URL. ALTERO_SMTP_URL (empty) Relay for outgoing mail, as smtp://[user:password@]host[:port] or smtps://…. Empty writes messages to the log. See Email. ALTERO_MAIL_FROM altero@localhost From address on outgoing mail. Set it to something the relay will send as.

items.title: Rate limiting and proxies
items.text: Setting Default What it does ALTERO_RATE_LIMIT 0 Requests allowed per API key, or per address when unauthenticated, in each window. Zero disables the limit. See Rate limiting. ALTERO_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW 60 Length of that window, in seconds. ALTERO_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS (empty) Proxies whose X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto may be believed, comma separated, or * for any peer. Only ever name a proxy that overwrites the header. See Behind a reverse proxy.

items.title: Retention
items.text:
The first three are also settable in Administration → Retention, and a value stored there wins over the value configured here. Zero means never. See Retention.

Setting Default What it does ALTERO_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 0 Days before permanent trash deletion; zero keeps trash indefinitely. ALTERO_ACTIVITY_RETENTION_DAYS 0 How long delivered group activity is kept. ALTERO_UPLOAD_RETENTION_HOURS 24 How long an authorized upload whose bytes never arrived is remembered. Nothing is lost by forgetting one; the client asks again. ALTERO_RETENTION_INTERVAL 0 How often, in seconds, to apply those periods. Zero means only altero retention run ever does. 3600 suits an instance that should not need asking.

items.title: Group notifications
items.text:
Nobody is subscribed until they ask, so these change nothing on an instance where no member has opted in. See Group notifications.

Setting Default What it does ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_QUIET_PERIOD 900 How long a group library must stop changing, in seconds, before what happened in it goes out. This is what turns one sync into one message rather than one per batch. ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_INTERVAL 60 How often, in seconds, to look for activity that has settled. Zero turns group notifications off; activity is still recorded.

items.title: Variables that are not settings
items.text:
These are read by something other than the application's own configuration, so they have no config.py equivalent.

Variable Read by What it does ALTERO_CONFIG the application Path to the configuration module, if not config.py at the repository root. ALTERO_SKIP_MIGRATIONS the container entrypoint 1 starts the server without running alembic upgrade head first. ALTERO_IMAGE_TAG docker/compose.yaml Which published image to run: latest, a chosen release tag, or dev for master. ALTERO_PUBLISH_PORT docker/compose.yaml Loopback port the API is published on. POSTGRES_PASSWORD docker/compose.yaml Password for the bundled PostgreSQL, used by both containers.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: This page covers running and operating altero. For a first local test, Getting started is shorter.

items.title: Choose how to run altero
items.text:
Method Best for Database Docker Compose Easiest evaluation and normal self-hosting PostgreSQL Source checkout Development or direct Python deployment SQLite by default; PostgreSQL optional

For a server used by several people, prefer PostgreSQL.

items.title: Database requirements
items.text:
The bundled container meets the requirements. For a source installation:

  • SQLite must support FTS5 with the trigram tokenizer. Migrations report an unsupported SQLite installation before proceeding.
  • PostgreSQL needs the pg_trgm and btree_gin extensions, usually provided by its contrib package.

Migrations create the PostgreSQL extensions when the database user has permission. Otherwise, ask the database administrator to run these in altero's database:

CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;
CREATE EXTENSION btree_gin;

Index creation can make a large library's first migration take longer and use additional disk space. A missing database feature stops the migration with an error.

items.title: Docker Compose
items.text:
The image is published as ghcr.io/eseifert/altero, so running altero needs no checkout and no build. The Compose file on its own is the deployment:

mkdir altero && cd altero
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eseifert/altero/master/docker/compose.yaml
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec altero altero user add <username>
docker compose exec altero altero user password <username>

From a repository checkout, name the file where it lives instead:

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml exec altero altero user add <username>
docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml exec altero altero user password <username>

The stack contains PostgreSQL, altero and persistent attachment storage.

altero user add creates the account without a password, so altero user password follows it. The alternative is to create the first account in the browser: registration is open while the instance has no accounts at all, and the account that claims it administers the instance. See Accounts.

The default latest image includes prereleases. For controlled upgrades, set ALTERO_IMAGE_TAG to your chosen release tag in .env beside the Compose file. Use dev only if you intend to follow development builds. The documentation site's latest alias is managed separately from the container tag.

The altero API is published on the loopback interface by default. Put a TLS terminator or reverse proxy in front of it rather than exposing the application port directly.

The Compose stack publishes container port 8000 at host port 8000. Set ALTERO_PUBLISH_PORT to change the host port; leave ALTERO_PORT unchanged unless you also update the container mapping.

items.title: Production settings to change first
items.text:
Before putting real data on the instance:

  1. Set a real POSTGRES_PASSWORD.
  2. Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL to the URL users will actually open.
  3. Terminate TLS in front of altero.
  4. Decide whether outgoing email is required; see Email.
  5. Name the reverse proxy in ALTERO_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS; see Behind a reverse proxy.

Put settings in .env beside your Compose file: docker/.env when using the repository layout.

To see the values Compose resolved:

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml config

items.title: Upgrade altero
items.text:
1. Read the changelog for changes between your installed and target releases. For older installations, also check historical upgrade notes.
  2. Back up the database, attachment storage and configuration together; see Backups.
  3. Update ALTERO_IMAGE_TAG if you pinned the image, then pull and recreate the application:
docker compose pull altero
docker compose up -d
  1. Check the logs and /health, then sync a test client before resuming normal use.

Run these commands beside a downloaded Compose file. In a repository checkout, add -f docker/compose.yaml to each Compose command.

Migrations run automatically when the container starts. On failure, the application exits instead of serving an incompatible database. Source installations must update dependencies, rebuild the browser interface and run uv run alembic upgrade head before restarting.

SMTP requires ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL; configure it before starting with email enabled. Single sign-on and passkeys also depend on a stable public address.

Some older upgrades rebuild search indexes or rename stored files. Allow time and free disk space. A rollback may require restoring both the database and storage backup; running an older image alone is not a recovery plan.

items.title: Update PostgreSQL within a major version
items.text:
The database has its own security updates; pulling only the altero image leaves it unchanged. Compose uses the moving postgres:18-alpine tag. After backing up the database and attachments, update it during a maintenance window:

docker compose stop altero
docker compose pull db
docker compose up -d --wait db
docker compose exec db psql -U altero -d altero -c 'SHOW server_version;'

Check the reported version against the release you intend to install before starting altero with docker compose up -d altero. In a checkout, add -f docker/compose.yaml to each command. Use your configured database user/name if you changed the defaults. A cached image or a registry still publishing an update can leave the database on an older version even after a pull. A minor update keeps the existing volume and needs neither pg_upgrade nor a reload.

The November 12, 2026 PostgreSQL update ships security and correctness fixes in 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20 and 14.25. PostgreSQL 14 has reached end of life; plan a major upgrade if you still use it. PostgreSQL 19 RC 2 is a prerelease, and is not the Compose or CI default.

Review the 18.7 release notes and the notes for your installed major version before restarting clients. altero's attachment full-text search uses a GIN index with gin_trgm_ops and btree_gin. If you suspect the GIN corruption described by upstream, rebuild that index after updating PostgreSQL, while altero is stopped:

docker compose exec db psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U altero -d altero \
    -c 'REINDEX INDEX ix_item_fulltext_library_content_trgm;'

Allow time and free disk space; this command blocks access to the table while rebuilding. The shipped schema has no GiST trigram indexes, partitioned tables or unconstrained bpchar columns, so those separate repair instructions apply only if you added them. For missing chunk number errors, upstream prescribes reindexing the affected table, including its TOAST index. If you use PostgreSQL incremental backups, take a new full backup after updating and base subsequent incrementals on it. These repairs are operator maintenance, not altero schema migrations; updating alone does not repair an already damaged index.

items.title: Upgrade PostgreSQL across a major version
items.text:
altero's migrations do not upgrade PostgreSQL's own on-disk data format.

Moving a PostgreSQL volume to a new major version requires a dump and restore, for example with pg_dump from the old server and psql into the new one. The PostgreSQL image will refuse an incompatible data directory rather than silently adopting it.

items.title: Build the image instead of pulling it
items.text:
To deploy local changes, build an image using the additional Compose file: docker/compose.build.yaml adds the build to the same deployment:

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml -f docker/compose.build.yaml up -d --build

The result is altero:local. It uses the same project and volumes as the pulled stack. Continue using both Compose files when operating a local build.

items.title: Try the image on its own
items.text:
For a quick single-user trial, the image runs without Compose or PostgreSQL:

docker run -d --name altero -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 -v altero-data:/data ghcr.io/eseifert/altero:latest
docker exec altero altero user add <username>
docker exec altero altero user password <username>

The SQLite database is kept on the /data volume, beside the attachments. ALTERO_DATABASE_URL selects another database, as the Compose stack does. For a server used by several people, use the Compose stack instead.

items.title: Podman
items.text:
The image runs under Podman unchanged. Three things differ from Docker.

It runs as UID 10001. /data inside the image belongs to that user. A named volume inherits the ownership; a bind mount arrives with the host's instead, and altero then cannot write attachments. Under rootless Podman, hand the directory to the mapped user before starting the container:

podman unshare chown -R 10001:10001 /srv/altero/storage

On SELinux systems, mount it with :Z so the container gets a matching label.

The port is the one above. The container's own health check follows ALTERO_PORT, so an instance that moves it stays healthy; publishing 8090:8000 on the host needs no ALTERO_PORT at all.

The health check needs the Docker image format. Podman reads a health check out of an image only in that format; an OCI image carries no such field, and podman healthcheck run then answers has no defined healthcheck. The published image uses the Docker format, but an image built locally does not unless it is asked to:

podman build --format docker -f docker/Dockerfile .

podman-compose runs docker/compose.yaml as it is. For Quadlet, a systemd unit or a NixOS virtualisation.oci-containers module, the settings are the ones Configuration lists, plus ALTERO_DATABASE_URL pointing at the PostgreSQL container over a shared network.

A worked NixOS example, with altero and PostgreSQL as virtualisation.oci-containers units on a shared Podman network, is posted in Discussion #5. It is one contributor's running configuration rather than a reference deployment.

For the tested configuration and its limits, see the recorded rootless Podman run. Use the same procedure to contribute another result.

items.title: From a source checkout
items.text:
Requirements:

  • A supported Python installation and uv. The required Python range and minimum uv release are declared in pyproject.toml.
  • Node and npm to build the browser interface. Use the Node release selected by web/.nvmrc.
  • A database meeting the requirements above.

Use current security updates for these tools.

Source installations also need ICU development libraries, pkg-config and a C++ compiler to build PyICU, used for duplicate PDF matching. On Debian or Ubuntu, install libicu-dev pkg-config g++ before uv sync. The Docker image includes the ICU runtime. See PyICU's installation instructions for other systems.

SQLite is the default. For PostgreSQL outside Docker, install the extra dependency:

uv sync --extra postgres

Check out your chosen release tag before installing; the default branch contains development work. For a basic SQLite installation:

git clone https://github.com/eseifert/altero.git
cd altero
git checkout <release-tag>
uv sync --locked
npm --prefix web ci
npm --prefix web run build
cp config.example.py config.py
uv run alembic upgrade head
uv run altero user add <username>
uv run altero user password <username>
uv run altero

The default address is:

http://127.0.0.1:8000

You can create an API key directly if needed:

uv run altero key add <username> --name laptop

The key is printed once and cannot be displayed again.

items.title: What a small instance costs
items.text:
Plan capacity for the application, database and growing attachment storage. Memory use depends on traffic and library size; account for PostgreSQL separately from the application process.

Attachment files are stored once per content digest even when several libraries use them. Administration → Storage shows physical disk use, library totals and missing files. Monitor free space and leave room for backups and migrations.

items.title: Attachment storage
items.text:
Use a normal filesystem that supports atomic renames for ALTERO_STORAGE_PATH. Local disks and suitable NFS or SMB mounts can provide this.

Warning

Do not use object storage mounted through s3fs, goofys or rclone as the attachment directory. Uploads rely on atomic renames, which these mounts do not provide. Back up a filesystem-based store to object storage instead.

items.title: Health check
items.text:
GET /health returns 200 and status: "ok" when the database is reachable. The response also reports the application, API and schema versions and migration revision. Use it for readiness monitoring.

An unavailable database returns 503 with {"status": "error"}. Inspect the server logs for details.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Settings come from three places, in increasing order of precedence: the built-in defaults, a config.py module, and ALTERO_-prefixed environment variables.

cp config.example.py config.py                  # a source installation
ALTERO_PORT=9000 ALTERO_DEBUG=true uv run altero  # or a one-off override

In the Compose stack, every ALTERO_ setting in docker/.env reaches the container.

Configuration lists every setting with its default, and how to set it in each of those places.

items.title: Public URL
items.text:
ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL should be the stable external URL of the instance, for example:

https://altero.example.org

API object links and attachment upload/download URLs use this address, including its HTTPS scheme, even when a reverse proxy connects to altero over HTTP. When it is unset, those URLs use the request's address instead.

It becomes required in practice when you use features that generate callbacks or bind credentials to a host:

  • OpenID Connect or SAML sign-in;
  • passkeys;
  • the authorization server, which refuses to serve its endpoints rather than guess the iss claim — see Connecting other applications;
  • SMTP, which refuses to start without it so account links cannot use an untrusted request host.

Changing the host of ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL invalidates existing passkeys. Changing only the scheme or port does not.

items.title: Outgoing email
items.text:
Email uses:

  • ALTERO_SMTP_URL;
  • ALTERO_MAIL_FROM; and
  • ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL.

Without an SMTP relay, most messages are written to the log instead. Self-service password reset is the exception: it is not enabled without a relay because a password-reset link must not be exposed in server logs.

See Email for relay URLs, Docker details, security notices and group digests.

items.title: Single sign-on
items.text:
OpenID Connect and SAML 2.0 providers are configured in Administration → Sign-in providers.

Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL first. The callback/redirect address shown in the administration screen is built from that value and must match the address registered with the identity provider.

See Administration.

items.title: Group notifications
items.text:
Group notifications are opt-in per member and per group.

Two settings control digest delivery:

ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_QUIET_PERIOD=900
ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_INTERVAL=60

ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_INTERVAL=0 disables delivery. Activity is still recorded, so it can be delivered after the feature is re-enabled.

See Email.

items.title: Behind a reverse proxy
items.text:
Configure your proxy to:

  • Accept attachment uploads at least as large as ALTERO_MAX_UPLOAD_MB (1 GiB by default). A smaller proxy limit produces 413 errors.
  • Pass WebSocket upgrades for /stream, used by Zotero Desktop.
  • Stream /web/libraries/<id>/events without buffering, used for live browser updates. Allow idle connections for at least a minute.
  • Preserve altero's security headers and cache controls. Do not cache /app/sw.js or /app/manifest.webmanifest beyond their revalidation rules.
  • Pass the external Host, and overwrite X-Forwarded-For with the actual client address.

Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL to the external HTTPS address. Set ALTERO_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to the connecting proxy's address so client IPs and schemes are recognized. Trust only a proxy that overwrites client-supplied forwarded headers. In a container network, this is usually a network address, not 127.0.0.1.

Run a single application process when using live updates: the desktop and browser notification brokers are process-local.

The examples below show routing. Configure your TLS certificates and security policy, including HSTS, at the proxy.

items.title: nginx
items.text:
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name zotero.example.org;

    # Attachments. The default is 1m, which rejects most PDFs with 413.
    client_max_body_size 1024m;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        # Overwritten, not appended: $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for would carry a
        # client-supplied header through, and altero believes this one.
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }

    # The streaming API. Same upstream, but the upgrade has to be passed on
    # explicitly and the connection lives longer than a request.
    location /stream {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
    }
}

items.title: Caddy
items.text:
zotero.example.org {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8000 {
        # Caddy appends the client to an X-Forwarded-For it was handed;
        # replacing it is what makes trusting the header safe.
        header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}
    }
}

Caddy needs nothing said about WebSockets or body size: it passes an upgrade through as it stands and imposes no limit of its own.

items.title: Traefik
items.text:
labels:
  - traefik.enable=true
  - traefik.http.routers.altero.rule=Host(`zotero.example.org`)
  - traefik.http.routers.altero.entrypoints=websecure
  - traefik.http.routers.altero.tls.certresolver=letsencrypt
  - traefik.http.services.altero.loadbalancer.server.port=8000

Traefik proxies the WebSocket without configuration and imposes no body limit. It replaces X-Forwarded-For with the address the connection came from unless forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs is set on the entry point, which is the behavior to keep.

Reaching altero by container name means both containers share a network, and the ports: publication in docker/compose.yaml is then unnecessary — remove it rather than exposing the application port beside the proxy.

items.title: Tailscale
items.text:
tailscale serve --bg 8000

tailscale serve terminates TLS for the machine's tailnet name, passes Host through, and sets X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For itself rather than appending to what the client sent. It connects from 127.0.0.1, so:

ALTERO_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=127.0.0.1
ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL=https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net

Under Docker Compose, altero sees the Docker network's gateway instead of 127.0.0.1; the access log shows the address to name.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.text:
The optional general request limiter is off by default. Password and second-factor sign-in have separate, always-on protection described below.

Example: allow 600 requests per 60 seconds per API key:

ALTERO_RATE_LIMIT=600 ALTERO_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW=60 uv run altero

Requests over the limit receive 429 with a whole-second Retry-After, which Zotero understands.

Unauthenticated requests are counted per client address. So are requests with a key that has not authenticated in the current window, as well as per key: made-up keys share their address's allowance. /health is never rate limited.

The limiter is process-local. With several application workers, each process has its own allowance. Use the reverse proxy or another edge component if you need a deployment-wide defensive limit.

items.title: Sign-in backoff
items.text:
Password and second-factor guesses have always-on protection shared across workers and restarts. The first five account attempts and twenty address attempts can proceed without waiting. Further guesses cause increasing pauses, up to five minutes. Responses include 429 and Retry-After; a quiet period of fifteen minutes resets the counters.

Username and email share the same account budget; changing aliases or requesting another code does not bypass it. Passkey and institutional sign-in do not use these password/code budgets.

Configure forwarded headers correctly so users behind a proxy are not all counted as one client address.

items.title: Moving or restoring data
items.text: For whole-library export/import, migration from zotero.org and recovery after recreating a database, see Administration.

items.title: Backups
items.text:
Keep the database and attachment storage as one consistent backup. Stop altero and other writers while taking it; for Compose, stop the application with docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml stop altero and leave PostgreSQL running. Use pg_dump for PostgreSQL, or copy the SQLite database while altero is stopped, and copy the attachment storage before restarting the application.

Keep configuration and the secrets needed to operate the instance with the backup. Test a restore in a separate instance before relying on it. A library archive preserves one library's data and files; it does not contain instance accounts or API keys.

items.title: The design system
items.text: For contributors styling the browser interface. Reuse shared tokens and styles from web/src/styles/ rather than defining a separate visual language per component.

items.title: The one rule
items.text:
Fill groups, outline controls, use hairlines between rows.

  • Cards, panels and callouts use a background fill without an enclosing border.
  • Operable controls use the outline color for boundaries.
  • Internal dividers use outline-variant; they do not enclose groups.

Use dialog.css for floating menus and dialogs.

items.title: Surfaces, in order
items.text:
Layer Token Shared class Page surface Page background Card, pane, block or table heading surface-container .card, .pane, .block, .table-head Inset or toolbar surface-container-high .card__inset, .toolbar Floating menu or dialog surface-container-high with shadow Rules in dialog.css

Do not use surface-container-low or -lowest. Use secondary-container for selection, error-container for errors and destructive warnings, and primary for the main action.

items.title: The card
items.text:
Import surfaces.css and use .card. Its shared recipe defines padding, spacing, rounding and fill.

Class Purpose .card__title Card heading .card__note Supporting text below a control .card__inset Nested content such as a newly issued key .card__warning Destructive warning, placed before its action .card--interactive A card that acts as a control .card__rows Rows separated by hairlines .pane A screen column whose contents arrange their own spacing .block A single content block such as a citation .chip A role or short status; use --warning for an unavailable state

Buttons within cards fit their labels rather than stretching across the card.

items.title: Tables
items.text:
Use a filled .table-head above rows on the page surface. .table-rows provides internal and closing hairlines. Put the divider on the line wrapper, so rows with checkboxes retain it.

Mark the current row with .row--current: selection fill and a bar on the leading edge. Selection must remain stronger than hover and recognizable without color alone.

items.title: Icon buttons and toolbars
items.text:
Group related icon actions in .toolbar, with plain .icon-button controls. A close button for the surrounding pane stays outside its content toolbar.

Use --on for an active toggle and --danger for destructive actions. Every icon-only control needs aria-label and title. Decorative icons beside text use aria-hidden.

items.title: Icons
items.text:
Edit SVG assets in web/src/assets/icons/: items/, sidebar/ and controls/. Use a 24-unit grid, rounded caps and joins, no fill, and the established stroke weight. Preserve viewBox, currentColor and descriptive <title> elements. Components set the display size.

Use the shared pencil for editing. Logos and favicons live separately in web/src/assets/.

items.title: Rows
items.text:
Use rows for navigation and actionable lists. Reuse SectionPanel.vue for settings and administration panels. Hover uses the shared translucent state layer; current rows use the selection fill.

Collection and tag counts use count-badge, with tabular digits and a neutral fill distinct from selection.

items.title: Spacing and shape
items.text:
Use --md-spacing-1 through -7: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 and 48 pixels. Card gaps use -3, space between cards uses -4, and card padding and page section gaps use -5.

Use corner-small for insets, corner-medium for cards, corner-full for pills, and the larger shared corners for dialogs.

items.title: Type
items.text:
Use the self-hosted IBM Plex fonts and shared type scale:

Token Use title-large Screen title title-medium Card title body-medium Body text body-small Supporting text, timestamps and counts label-medium Chips

Avoid custom sizes and text transforms. Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums for aligned numbers. See font loading.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text:
The target is WCAG AA. The checks below cover measurable parts; the interface has not had a full accessibility audit or screen-reader verification.

  • Contrast: at least 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for identifying control boundaries and focus indicators.
  • Status: accompany color with text, shape or semantics. Errors use role="alert"; toggles use aria-pressed.
  • Focus: use the shared visible ring. Keep focused content clear of the sticky header and restore focus after closing dialogs.
  • Targets: at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels; grow touch controls for coarse pointers.
  • Alternatives: provide controls for every drag operation. Use logical start/end CSS so direction changes work.
