  • Authentication: permit pasting, including into one-time-code inputs. Do not add puzzles or transcription tasks.
  • Motion: use shared transitions in motion.css and respect prefers-reduced-motion. Press feedback must not move its target.
  • Messages: keep toast announcements in a persistent live region. Pause expiry while pointer or keyboard focus is on the toast, independently.

Loading skeletons follow the list's structure and accompany an accessible status message. Undo messages supplement Trash/Restore; they are not the only way to recover a trashed item.

The item list uses buttons rather than a grid, so screen readers hear values without column names. Review this tradeoff during assistive-technology testing.

items.title: What keeps this
items.text:
Check Protects surfaces.node.spec.ts Shared surfaces, allowed layers and divider use contrast.node.spec.ts Text/control contrast and selection stronger than hover fonts.node.spec.ts Self-hosted fonts logical.node.spec.ts Logical CSS properties; existing physical declarations may only decrease Browser tests with axe Serious and critical findings at desktop and phone sizes

Review explicit guard exceptions before adding one. Passing automated checks does not establish complete accessibility or support in every browser.

items.title: Email
items.text: altero can run without an SMTP relay. Configure email only if your instance needs messages delivered to users rather than written to the server log.

items.title: Do you need a mail relay?
items.text:
Feature Without SMTP With SMTP Email confirmation Link written to log Delivered by email Group invitations Available in-app for existing accounts; link can be logged Delivered by email Administrator-issued password link Link shown to administrator Also delivered by email when possible Self-service password reset Unavailable Available when enabled Email second-factor code Not useful without delivery Delivered by email Security notices Not delivered Delivered to confirmed addresses Group activity digests In-app notification still exists Optional email copy

Most messages fall back to the log when no relay is configured. Without ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL, account links in these logs and administrator-issued reset links are relative paths: prepend the instance's trusted external address before opening or sharing one. Self-service password reset does not fall back to logs, because a password-setting link should not be exposed to anyone who can read server logs.

items.title: Messages altero sends
items.text:
altero sends plain-text mail for:

  • confirming an email address;
  • group invitations;
  • password-setting links;
  • email second-factor codes;
  • password-change notices;
  • second-factor change notices; and
  • opt-in group activity digests.

Security notices are sent only to a confirmed email address.

Confirmation links are valid for 24 hours. Administrator-issued or self-service password links are single-use and valid for 12 hours. Email sign-in codes are valid for ten minutes, work once and are tied to the browser session that requested them.

For reset links issued before a public-address correction, see historical upgrade notes.

items.title: Run without SMTP
items.text:
With ALTERO_SMTP_URL unset, altero logs messages at WARNING instead of sending them.

For Docker Compose, find a logged message with:

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml logs altero | grep -A8 'was not sent'

This is a supported operating mode. An account with an unconfirmed address can still sign in, synchronize and use its library.

What you lose is external delivery: security notices, useful email-code authentication, self-service password reset and invitations to people who do not yet have an account on the instance.

items.title: Configure an SMTP relay
items.text:
Set three values:

Setting Environment variable Purpose SMTP_URL ALTERO_SMTP_URL SMTP relay and optional credentials MAIL_FROM ALTERO_MAIL_FROM Sender address PUBLIC_URL ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL Base URL used in links

Example:

ALTERO_SMTP_URL='smtp://altero%40example.org:s3cret@mail.example.org:587' \
ALTERO_MAIL_FROM='altero <altero@example.org>' \
ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL='https://altero.example.org' \
    uv run altero

Equivalent config.py values:

SMTP_URL = "smtp://altero%40example.org:s3cret@mail.example.org:587"
MAIL_FROM = "altero <altero@example.org>"
PUBLIC_URL = "https://altero.example.org"

Invalid SMTP URLs are rejected when configuration is loaded, so configuration errors appear at startup rather than only when a user is waiting for mail.

items.title: SMTP URL format
items.text:
smtp://[username[:password]@]host[:port]
smtps://[username[:password]@]host[:port]
  • smtp:// defaults to port 587 and attempts STARTTLS.
  • smtps:// defaults to port 465 and uses TLS from the start.

With smtp://, if the relay does not offer STARTTLS, altero logs a warning and can continue in clear text. That can be acceptable for a relay on the same trusted host or container network. Over a network you do not control, prefer smtps://.

items.title: Encode credentials in the URL
items.text:
Usernames and passwords are URL components. Characters such as @, :, /, #, ? and % must be percent-encoded.

For example:

altero@example.org  →  altero%40example.org

A relay that needs no authentication can omit credentials:

SMTP_URL = "smtp://localhost:25"

items.title: Sender address
items.text:
ALTERO_MAIL_FROM accepts either a bare address or a display name plus address.

Use an address the relay is allowed to send as. SPF, DKIM and DMARC configuration belongs to the mail provider or relay; altero only authenticates to the relay and hands it the message.

The default altero@localhost is a placeholder, not a deliverable production address.

items.title: Public URL
items.text:
Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL to the external address users can open, for example:

https://altero.example.org

This is required when ALTERO_SMTP_URL is set; altero refuses to start without it. Password-reset, email-confirmation and invitation links never use the request's Host or forwarded host headers. Self-service reset also requires this setting before it issues a token or offers the form.

ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL is separate from ALTERO_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS: the first controls generated public links and callback addresses, while the second names the proxies whose forwarded client address and scheme altero believes.

items.title: Docker Compose
items.text:
Put mail settings in .env beside the Compose file (docker/.env in a checkout). See Configuration.

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=something-other-than-the-default
ALTERO_SMTP_URL=smtps://altero%40example.org:s3cret@mail.example.org
ALTERO_MAIL_FROM=altero@example.org
ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL=https://altero.example.org

Then restart and inspect the resolved configuration:

docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml config | grep ALTERO_

items.title: Common Docker mistakes
items.text:
Keep .env beside the Compose file. A checkout uses docker/.env; a downloaded deployment usually uses .env in its working directory.

Escape $ for Compose. In .env, Compose interpolates $NAME. Double a literal dollar sign as $$. This is in addition to URL percent-encoding.

Example password p@ss$1 inside the SMTP URL:

p%40ss$$1

Remember that localhost means the container. A relay on the Docker host can be reached through host.docker.internal when the host relay is listening on an address reachable from the container network.

items.title: Group notifications
items.text:
Group activity email is opt-in. Every member starts unsubscribed.

A user can independently subscribe to these categories for each group:

Category Examples Items added or changed New item, title edit Items deleted Trashed or permanently removed People joining or leaving Membership changes Collections added or changed Group-library organization

items.title: Digest timing
items.text:
Zotero uploads can contain many writes. Sending mail for every write would create a flood, so altero waits until the group has been quiet and sends one digest for the accumulated activity.

Environment variable Default Meaning ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_QUIET_PERIOD 900 Seconds the library must be quiet before a digest is ready ALTERO_GROUP_DIGEST_INTERVAL 60 How often the server looks for ready digests; 0 disables delivery

A member does not receive a digest about changes they caused themselves.

The email contains counts, not item titles. Detailed activity remains in the authenticated web interface so library contents are not unnecessarily copied into mail systems and logs.

Digest processing is coordinated in the database, so several application workers do not send the same digest twice.

There is no retry queue. If a relay refuses a digest, altero logs the failure and still keeps the in-app notification.

items.title: Check mail delivery
items.text:
The quickest real test is an email-confirmation message:

  1. Sign in with an account whose address is unconfirmed.
  2. Use Resend in the confirmation notice.
  3. Check the altero log for an SMTP error.
  4. Check the recipient mailbox.

A successful handoff to the SMTP relay does not guarantee delivery to the final inbox.

For a local SMTP sink:

uvx --from aiosmtpd python -m aiosmtpd -n -l localhost:8025
ALTERO_SMTP_URL=smtp://localhost:8025 ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8000 uv run altero

This prints received messages instead of sending real mail.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text:
Mail failure does not roll back the action that caused the message. For example, a password change remains a password change even if the security notice cannot be delivered.

Failures are logged. There is no mail queue and no automatic retry. Most user-triggered messages can be requested again.

SMTP requests time out after ten seconds. Check relay connectivity if delivery stalls.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
This guide runs altero locally and connects a test Zotero Desktop profile. For an existing server, go straight to Connecting a Zotero client.

Warning

Use a separate Zotero profile or a library you can recreate. Keep a current backup of important libraries and don’t rely on altero as your only copy yet.

items.title: 1. Start altero
items.text:
With Docker and Docker Compose installed, run:

mkdir altero && cd altero
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eseifert/altero/master/docker/compose.yaml
docker compose up -d

This starts altero and PostgreSQL, with persistent storage. The server is available only on your computer at http://localhost:8000. The default image tag is latest, which includes prereleases.

For source installation, Podman, or a server other people can reach, see Deployment.

items.title: 2. Create your account
items.text:
Open http://localhost:8000/app/ and register. The first account administers the instance; public registration then closes unless an administrator enables it.

Alternatively, create an account from the shell:

docker compose exec altero altero user add <username>
docker compose exec altero altero user password <username>

Run both commands: user add does not set a password.

items.title: 3. Configure Zotero Desktop
items.text:
In your test profile, open Settings → Advanced → Config Editor and set:

extensions.zotero.api.url = http://localhost:8000/
extensions.zotero.streaming.url = ws://localhost:8000/stream

Keep the trailing slash on the API URL. Restart Zotero.

Important

Set both URLs. Leaving the streaming URL unchanged can send your altero API key to zotero.org.

A profile that has already synced needs special care. Read A profile that has synced before before connecting it.

items.title: 4. Link the account
items.text:
Open Settings → Sync → Link Account in Zotero. Sign in to altero in the browser window that opens and approve the connection.

Create an item, a collection and an attachment in Zotero. Sync, then open altero's browser interface to check that they arrived.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Connect a second client to check synchronization in both directions.
  • Use the browser interface to manage your library.
  • Prepare a server for everyday use, including HTTPS and backups.
  • Check features and limits, including mobile-app support.

items.title: Why altero exists
items.text: altero is for people and organizations that need the Zotero synchronization service on infrastructure they control. Libraries, notes, annotations, group data and attachments can stay on their own server.

items.title: Why not just WebDAV?
items.text:
WebDAV stores attachment files for a personal Zotero library. Library data still synchronizes through zotero.org, and group files cannot use WebDAV.

altero provides both data and file synchronization for personal and group libraries. It works with unmodified Zotero Desktop. Its browser interface also supports everyday reference management.

items.title: What running your own server involves
items.text:
A basic installation has one application, a database and an attachment directory. SQLite suits small personal installations; PostgreSQL suits concurrent users. No separate search service, cache or queue is required.

You take responsibility for hosting, HTTPS, backups, upgrades and account management. The browser provides routine administration, including storage reports and retention settings. Institutional sign-in and finer group permissions can help a shared installation fit local needs.

An instance administrator manages the installation without automatically gaining access to everybody's library contents.

items.title: Compatibility comes first
items.text:
The normal Zotero desktop application must be able to exchange changes through altero. When published API documentation and actual server behavior disagree, altero follows the behavior clients depend on. Additional features must preserve that compatibility.

Mobile apps need a separate build pointed at altero because they do not offer a server setting. altero does not distribute such builds. See Mobile apps.

items.title: Is altero right for you?
items.text:
Hosted synchronization at zotero.org remains convenient and supports Zotero's development. altero is an independent project for users who need another deployment model; it is not supported by Zotero.

Keep a current backup of important libraries and don’t rely on altero as your only copy yet. Read What works for capabilities and limits, then try a local instance with disposable data.

items.title: Connecting other applications
items.text:
Operators can register applications that need limited access to an altero library. Users approve each application in their browser and can disconnect it later. The application receives expiring tokens instead of a password or long-lived API key.

This is separate from institutional sign-in. Zotero Desktop still uses an API key; browser sessions never authenticate the Zotero API.

items.title: Registering an application
items.text:
Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL to the stable external HTTPS address first. Register the application from the server shell:

uv run altero oauth add notebook \
    --name "Notebook" \
    --description "Reads your library into a notebook" \
    --redirect-uri https://notebook.example.com/auth/callback \
    --scope openid --scope profile --scope library.read --scope files.read

Repeat --redirect-uri and --scope as needed. The registered scopes are a ceiling: the application can request these or fewer. Applications cannot register themselves.

For a server application that can protect a secret, add --confidential. Copy the secret when it is printed; it cannot be shown again. For logout redirects, register each address with --post-logout-redirect-uri.

uv run altero oauth list
uv run altero oauth disable notebook
uv run altero oauth rotate-key

Disabling stops the application for everyone. Key rotation changes the key used to sign new ID tokens while retaining verification keys for older tokens.

items.title: Redirect URIs
items.text:
Use absolute URIs without fragments. HTTPS is required except for loopback addresses and native-app private schemes such as com.example.app:/callback. Matching is exact, including path and query.

For a native app's loopback callback, the port may vary: registering http://127.0.0.1:1/callback permits another port at that same host and path. localhost and [::1] have the same exception.

items.title: What an application gets
items.text:
Access tokens last one hour; refresh tokens last thirty days. Send an access token with each API request:

GET /users/1/items HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer alt_at_…
Scope Permission openid Identify the account; no library access profile Read its display name and username email Read its email address and confirmation status groups Read group names; no group-library contents library.read Read personal-library items, collections, searches and tags library.write Add, change and remove personal-library objects notes.read Include notes in readable libraries files.read Download attachment bytes groups.read Read group libraries the account belongs to groups.write Write to those group libraries

library.write requires library.read; groups.write requires groups.read. notes.read and files.read require library.read. Unknown, unregistered or incomplete scope combinations are refused.

Notes without permission disappear from listings and direct reads. Without file permission, attachment metadata and extracted full text remain readable, but file downloads are refused. Public-library note access has an exception; see credential restrictions. Group policies and member restrictions continue to apply to tokens.

items.title: Where a grant reaches
items.text:
On the consent screen, the user can allow all resources covered by the scopes or select particular libraries and collections. Applications cannot choose or widen that selection.

A collection grant includes its subcollections and items filed there later, plus child notes, attachments and annotations. It does not include unfiled items or objects filed only elsewhere. Restricted collection grants cannot read saved searches, settings or deletion logs, or change library structure. Items inside the grant remain writable when scopes permit; new items must be filed within it.

Restrictions persist when tokens are refreshed. Approving again replaces the grant rather than accumulating access. Deleting its last selected collection does not turn a restricted grant into unrestricted access. API keys are unaffected. See resource restrictions for endpoint behavior.

items.title: The flow
items.text:
The following sections are for application developers. Use discovery and an OAuth/OpenID client library where possible. Authorization code requires PKCE with S256 for every client, including confidential clients.

  1. Generate a verifier, its challenge, and a random state value.
  2. Open the authorization endpoint in the user's browser:
/oauth/authorize
  ?client_id=notebook
  &redirect_uri=https://notebook.example.com/auth/callback
  &response_type=code
  &scope=openid%20profile%20library.read
  &state=<random-value>
  &code_challenge=<BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))>
  &code_challenge_method=S256
  &nonce=<optional-nonce>
  1. The user signs in and reviews consent in altero. At the callback, verify state before exchanging the code.
  2. Exchange the code on the back channel:
curl -X POST https://library.example.org/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d client_id=notebook \
  -d code=... \
  -d code_verifier=... \
  -d redirect_uri=https://notebook.example.com/auth/callback

The response contains access_token, token_type, expires_in, refresh_token and scope, plus an id_token when openid was granted.

items.title: Presenting a client secret
items.text:
Public clients send no secret. Confidential clients authenticate every token request using HTTP Basic or a client_secret form field. Never send the secret both ways in one request. If Basic and a form client_id are both present, they must identify the same client.

Discovery advertises none, client_secret_basic and client_secret_post.

items.title: Refresh and replay
items.text:
curl -X POST https://library.example.org/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token -d client_id=notebook -d refresh_token=alt_rt_...

Confidential clients also supply their secret. Replace the saved refresh token after each successful refresh. Reusing a spent refresh token or authorization code revokes the token family, including when concurrent requests race. The application must start authorization again.

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
Endpoint Purpose /.well-known/openid-configuration OpenID discovery /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server OAuth discovery /oauth/authorize Browser authorization /oauth/token Code exchange, refresh and device polling /oauth/revoke Token revocation /oauth/userinfo Claims allowed by the scopes /oauth/jwks.json ID-token verification keys /oauth/logout End the browser session /oauth/device_authorization Start authorization on a device without a browser

Revocation uses the same client authentication methods as the token endpoint. Revoking an access token leaves its refresh token usable; revoking a refresh token invalidates its family. Unknown tokens receive a successful response; clients cannot revoke another application's tokens.

items.title: A device with no browser
items.text:
Post client_id and scope to /oauth/device_authorization. Show the returned user_code and verification_uri, or open verification_uri_complete on another device. Keep device_code private.

Poll /oauth/token with:

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code
&client_id=notebook&device_code=...

Respect the returned interval. Device codes expire after ten minutes.

Response Action authorization_pending Continue polling at the allowed interval slow_down Increase the interval access_denied Stop; the user refused expired_token Stop and start a new request if needed Tokens Save them; the device code is spent

Confidential clients authenticate while polling. Device authorization uses no PKCE or redirect, but registration still requires a redirect URI. The first completed consent decision stands.

items.title: Signing out
items.text:
Send the browser to /oauth/logout using GET or POST with a required id_token_hint. An optional post_logout_redirect_uri must match a registered logout address; state is returned there.

The hint must be a token altero signed for the signed-in account. An expired hint is accepted. Logout ends the browser session but leaves the application's grant and tokens usable. To withdraw access, disconnect the application in Settings or revoke its tokens.

items.title: ID tokens
items.text:
Tokens use RS256. Verify them with /oauth/jwks.json and the issuer from discovery. Claims include iss, sub, aud, iat, exp, auth_time and at_hash, plus a requested nonce and granted identity claims.

Use sub as the stable account identifier. Email and group names are not identifiers; group names are not unique. The groups claim is an empty list when no groups apply. Resource restrictions also narrow that list.

The issuer comes only from ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL. These endpoints refuse to operate without it. Signing keys persist in the database.

items.title: What a person sees
items.text:
The consent page names the application, explains its permissions, highlights new permissions, and offers library or collection restrictions. Users sign in through their usual password, passkey or institutional provider first.

Settings → Connected applications shows permissions and restrictions. Disconnecting revokes access immediately.

items.title: Interoperability checks
items.text: Authlib exercises live flows in CI. The recorded OpenID Foundation assessment passed Config OP but did not pass Basic OP, partly because it omits the PKCE challenge altero requires. altero is not OpenID-certified. Read the results and limits before depending on an OpenID feature.

items.title: Security notes
items.text:
Tokens never bypass the account's own permissions. Suspension stops token access along with other credentials. /keys/current and key-management routes refuse access tokens; use grant disconnection or token revocation instead.

Credentials and codes are stored as hashes. Expired authorization records are removed by the retention sweep. See the compatibility decisions for the authentication boundary and deliberate protocol choices.

items.title: OpenID provider interoperability
items.text: Historical local assessment on 2026-10-31, using altero at d06783c: the OpenID Foundation suite's Config OP passed. Basic OP did not pass. This is a development assessment, not OpenID certification or an exhaustive claim of protocol support. The mandatory S256 PKCE policy was retained.

items.title: Independent client in CI
items.text:
Run the independent Authlib client checks with:

uv run pytest -q tests/test_authlib.py

They cover code and PKCE, public/confidential clients, ID tokens, userinfo, refresh, replay, revocation, device consent and logout over live HTTP. No external provider is required. Keep loopback port 18765 free.

The harness approves through real cookie/CSRF routes, without testing consent page rendering or a separate client callback listener. See the fixture scope.

items.title: Foundation suite environment
items.text:
The official conformance suite reported version 5.3.4, tag release-v5.3.4, revision e8d5167. The reviewed source checkout was e8d5167c84f1913a137c260f7ee991f03908ce8f. The downloaded images were pinned by digest:

mongo@sha256:b9924c330a8bbc5800fe9c69f04a84e221eca7b28fd049a0354147d9908fa142

MongoDB belongs to the suite and stores its plans and results. altero used SQLite; it gained no MongoDB dependency. Both containers were disposable and bound only to loopback, with MongoDB on 27174 and the suite on HTTPS 18084. The suite ran its development profile with its dummy local administrator. This configuration is for isolated testing, never a public deployment.

altero served HTTPS on 18766 with public_url=https://127.0.0.1:18766 and a fresh test account. A short-lived local certificate covered 127.0.0.1 and localhost; the suite's Java trust store and the httpx2 driver trusted it. Chromium accepted this local certificate when executing the suite's callback JavaScript and capturing its requested error-page screenshots. No production accounts, identity providers or library databases were used.

items.title: Repeating the assessment
items.text:
Use the official suite's local Docker instructions with the pinned image above and an isolated database. Configure HTTPS for the suite and altero, trust the test CA in Java, and set altero's public URL to its actual issuer. Register two confidential clients through altero oauth add, both with scopes openid profile email and the suite's exact callback: https://127.0.0.1:18084/test/a/altero/callback for alias altero in this run.

In the suite configuration, set server.discoveryUrl to altero's discovery URL. Supply client and client2 objects with their respective client_id, client_secret and scope. Also supply client_secret_post with the first client's values: the Basic plan uses that separate object for its form-secret module. An absent object is a setup failure, not protocol evidence.

Run oidcc-config-certification-test-plan with its fixed defaults. Run oidcc-basic-certification-test-plan with server_metadata=discovery and client_registration=static_client; the plan fixes response type, mode and authentication method per module. Follow its actual authorization URLs, authenticate the disposable account, approve consent where offered, and run the suite's callback JavaScript. Upload the requested real error screenshots. Do not insert PKCE into the suite's requests or relax altero's PKCE requirement to turn this profile green.

Retain raw plans, per-module logs and screenshots privately: suite exports contain client secrets, session cookies and tokens. Publish only sanitized results. The local assessment retained these under /tmp/altero-p74-oidf; the containers and live server were stopped afterwards. The hosted Authlib result is linked above; the Foundation assessment itself remains a local run.

items.title: Release validation history
items.text: These are historical records, not results for the current checkout. Keep the release, client and tool versions attached to each result. For current operation, use Deployment; for new release checks, use the release checklist.

items.title: Historical upgrade notes
items.text:
Read the changelog for every release between your installed and target versions. These notes retain requirements that may matter when upgrading an older instance.

Starting point or target Action or effect alpha.3 or earlier Upgrading advances group-library versions once so desktops refresh cached permissions. Personal-library versions are unchanged. beta.2 or earlier The upgrade builds a full-text index. Allow additional time and disk space. beta.5 or earlier The first start reads and hashes attachment storage and renames snapshots by their archive digest. Keep free space for the largest snapshot if hard links are unavailable. Downgrading requires restoring storage as well as the database. beta.6 to beta.7 No database or storage migration was required. beta.8 with SMTP Set ALTERO_PUBLIC_URL before starting; SMTP without a public URL is refused. Account links no longer use request host headers. beta.8 child-item repair Child notes and attachments incorrectly filed in collections are repaired and receive new versions. Sync every desktop afterwards. Parents and attachment bytes remain intact. OIDC issuer saved under beta.7 If its trailing slash was removed, re-save the exact issuer from provider discovery after upgrading. Existing values cannot be repaired automatically.

An old password-reset message with an incorrect host is not revoked by upgrading. After setting the public URL, issue a fresh reset in Administration → Accounts to replace the account's previous token.

  • Pinned Zotero and dataserver source verification (30 client functions), plus the network-consumer review gate: 324 files, 88 consumers, no parse errors or stale reviews.
  • Ruff formatting/lint, Ty, the locked dependency check and strict documentation build.
  • Upgrades from beta.5: both migrations apply to a SQLite database created and filled by beta.5, and alembic check finds no drift. The first start renamed the stored web snapshot to the digest of its own bytes and a second start left it alone. Items with their versions, the library version, a setting, a deletion record, a search for über and both files' download headers and bytes were identical before and after, and a write moved the library on by one version.
  • The wheel built through the source archive: all 587 browser files survived, and real HTTP from the extracted wheel served /health (1.0.0b6), /app/ with its Content-Security-Policy, the index's assets and a font, and the service worker and manifest with no-cache. Authenticated API reads and writes passed, with sandbox and nosniff on their answers, and a file uploaded by the three-step protocol downloaded with the same bytes.

The recorded desktop matrix has 68 SQLite/PostgreSQL combinations and 794 phases with Zotero 10.0.6 on Linux, run against the release candidate: all 34 scenarios pass on both databases, each database in a single run. Remote CI and multi-architecture image publication must still be checked after pushing.

items.title: Database schema
items.text: For contributors changing persistence or synchronization. This reference lists storage choices that affect API behavior. For migration commands, see the development guide.

items.title: Adopted from the dataserver
items.text:
Tag type belongs to the tag. tags is unique on (libraryID, name, type), so a name added by hand and the same name added by a translator are two rows rather than one tag with two links. Tags also carry an eight-character key, like every other syncable object.

Three timestamps per object. dateAdded and dateModified are supplied by the client and round-trip through the API; serverDateModified is set by the server on every write. Keeping them apart is what makes the serverDateModified sort trustworthy — a client cannot reorder another client's results by backdating its own dateModified. Applied to items, collections, saved searches and tags via the Timestamped mixin in altero/db.py.

Versions start at 1, not 0, matching DEFAULT '1' on every versioned table.

Collections and searches are trashable. The dataserver has deletedCollections and deletedSearches alongside deletedItems, so the trash is not an item-only concept.

items.title: Deliberate differences
items.text:
Pending registration requests are separate from accounts. The registration_requests table is persistence for the planned verified-email and administrator-approval workflow. It stores no password or usable credential and creates no user or library. That public workflow is not enabled yet.

Pending rows reserve a canonical username and email address through unique, nullable columns. Terminal rows release both reservations while retaining the request's original fields. Constraints require email proof before review, decision actor/time for approval or rejection, and an account ID for approval. Actor and account IDs are historical values without foreign keys, so deleting an account does not erase the recorded decision. They grant no access.

Internal submission defaults to disabled. When explicitly enabled by a trusted caller, it normalizes the requested name/address, checks existing accounts and reserves both values atomically. Requests expire at their deadline, releasing both reservations while keeping history. Activation must recheck availability; a pending reservation cannot override an account provisioned by an operator.

Verification recording accepts only a live email-pending request and the exact normalized address its trusted mailbox-proof consumer verified. A replay cannot refresh the proof or extend the deadline. After the caller authenticates the applicant, cancellation releases either pending state; terminal history cannot be reopened. Conditional updates resolve concurrent transitions. Cleanup shares their transaction so a failed transition does not commit only part of the operation. These are internal primitives; applicant sessions and public routes remain to be wired.

An email-pending request can store one outstanding mailbox proof: a unique SHA-256 token digest, the recipient address and an expiry no later than the request deadline. The raw link token is never stored. All three proof fields are present together or absent together; later states cannot retain them. This internal issuer returns the stored recipient and a fresh random token, retaining only its SHA-256 digest. Resending replaces the old proof without extending the request deadline. A link lasts at most 24 hours; equality with either expiry deadline is already too late.

Proof consumption checks the digest, saved recipient against the current address, request state and both deadlines in one conditional update. The same update clears the proof and moves the request to review; concurrent consumers have one winner. Cancellation, expiry and trusted verification recording also clear any outstanding token. A failed transaction preserves the earlier link and lifecycle state together. These helpers send no mail and grant no account or library access; delivery, resend limits and applicant authorization still need caller integration.

The internal gated-registration policy requires configured SMTP and an absolute HTTP(S) public_url, and refuses SSO-only mode. It retains neither the settings nor relay credentials. Allowed domains are normalized to lowercase ASCII DNS names, with duplicates removed. An empty list allows any valid DNS domain; otherwise matching is exact, and every allowed subdomain must be listed. Wildcards, trailing dots and Unicode domain spellings are refused; use the domain's ASCII punycode spelling in both the policy and the address. Existing account address handling is unchanged. Mailbox verification proves control of an address, not current institutional membership. This internal policy has no operator setting or public caller yet, and does not prove the relay is reachable. Submission and trusted verification recording require this policy explicitly. Proof issuance and consumption apply its current domain ceiling in their conditional updates, so a link issued under an older allowlist cannot advance an ineligible request. Refused issuance leaves the earlier link intact; refused consumption does not spend it. Restoring eligibility can make a still-live link usable again. Cancellation and expiry remain available without an admission policy. Final activation must recheck the policy as well as identity availability.

An authenticated applicant's internal mailbox-change operation also checks the current policy and refuses addresses held by existing accounts or other pending requests. A changed address reserves the new mailbox and releases the old one in the same update, clears outstanding proofs and earlier verification, and returns either pending state to email-pending. It keeps the original request deadline. An unchanged normalized address preserves its proof/review state; terminal requests cannot be reopened. Conflicting reservations and failed commits preserve the previous mailbox and proof together. The caller must authenticate the applicant before using this operation; the row ID alone grants no authority.

The trash is a flag, not a table. The dataserver records trashed objects in deletedItems(itemID, dateDeleted); altero uses a deleted boolean on the object. The queries are equivalent and the flag avoids a join on every listing. The cost is that the deletion time is not kept, which nothing in the v3 API exposes.

Creators are not deduplicated. The dataserver interns creators in a creators table and links them through itemCreators, so one person shared by a thousand items is stored once. altero stores creators inline on the item. This trades space for simplicity; deduplication can be introduced behind the same service functions if it ever matters.

Notes and attachments are not separate tables. The dataserver keeps itemNotes (with a sanitized copy and an 80-character derived title) and itemAttachments. altero stores both a note's content and an attachment's storage columns as ordinary field rows in item_fields. Those fields are not in the published schema, so the set each type accepts is declared in UNLISTED_FIELDS in services/itemwrites.py rather than derived.

The upside is that one code path stores every field of every item type. The cost is that nothing at the database level constrains an attachment to have a linkMode, where a dedicated table would.

Relations belong to objects. Items and collections each have relation rows that produce their API relations maps. This differs from upstream's general library-scoped relation table.

Sort keys are columns on the item. The dataserver keeps itemSortFields (sortTitle truncated to 79 characters, plus creatorSummary) in a side table and joins itemData for date sorting. altero keeps sort_title, sort_creator and sort_date on items, untruncated, so every sort is a single-table index scan.

No sharding. shards, shardHosts and shardLibraries have no counterpart: the dataserver spreads libraries across MySQL servers, and altero uses one database.

Files are stored by digest. Identical registered bytes are stored once at <storage>/<first two digest characters>/<digest>. Upload authorizations live in storage_uploads until registration. Each attachment records its registered file separately from client-supplied metadata, so a claimed digest does not confer access to another library's bytes.

Deleting an item does not immediately remove its stored bytes. Administrators can remove unreferenced and abandoned staging files from Storage, with a grace period protecting uploads in progress.

The item type schema is not in the database. The dataserver stores item types, fields and their mappings in master.sql tables (itemTypes, fields, baseFieldMappings, …). altero reads them from the vendored schema.json instead, which keeps them in step with the published schema and out of migrations. Item types and field names are therefore stored as strings rather than as foreign keys to an ID table.

items.title: Tables with no direct counterpart
items.text:
write_tokens records a Zotero-Write-Token for as long as a client might retry with it, so a repeated request does not create the objects twice. The dataserver caches these outside the database.

item_fulltext holds the text a client extracted from an attachment, matching the dataserver's table of the same purpose, without the reindexing bookkeeping that a hosted service needs.

settings stores sync setting values as JSON text rather than separate modeled fields.

items.title: Delete log
items.text: syncDeleteLogKeys(libraryID, objectType, key, timestamp, version) backs /deleted?since=, with objectType one of collection, creator, item, relation, search, setting, tag or tagName. Its primary key is (libraryID, objectType, key), so deleting a key that was deleted before updates the existing row rather than adding a second one. altero mirrors this shape in deleted_objects.

items.title: Concurrency
items.text:
Writes to one library are serialized by taking a row lock on it before the version precondition is checked and holding it until commit, so a request is atomic with respect to its library. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is emitted on PostgreSQL and dropped on SQLite, which has a single writer anyway. The version increment itself is computed by the database rather than in Python, so it stays correct even without the lock.

Write-token and tag get-or-create operations use unique constraints rather than a separate existence check followed by insertion. This preserves their correctness independently of library locking.

SQLite is configured with foreign_keys=ON, WAL and a busy timeout. BEGIN IMMEDIATE is deliberately not used: it would close the remaining lock-upgrade hole, but takes the write lock for read-only transactions too, so a single long read would block every writer. A deployment serving several clients at once should use PostgreSQL.

items.title: What works
items.text:
Use this page to check whether altero supports your workflow. For installation, start with Getting started.

Ordinary Zotero Desktop synchronization is the main target. Automated desktop acceptance runs on Linux. Basic sync has community reports on Windows and macOS; broader conflict and recovery coverage on those platforms remains unverified. Mobile apps need a separate build pointed at your server.

Keep a current backup of important libraries and don’t rely on altero as your only copy yet. Recorded results and their limits are in desktop compatibility checks, Podman testing and release validation history.

items.title: User-facing capabilities
items.text: Capability Status Notes Zotero Desktop synchronization ✅ Items, collections, tags, saved searches and deletions Notes and annotations ✅ Included in normal item synchronization Attachment file sync ✅ Files stored once per digest Full-text upload and search ✅ Uses the database rather than Elasticsearch Group libraries ✅ Includes group policy and membership My Publications ✅ Includes browser publishing and profile pages Citations and bibliographies ✅ CSL-based styles and Zotero-compatible formats Zotero export formats ✅ API and browser export support Browser interface ✅ Library browsing, item and note editing, file uploads, account settings, groups and administration; installable as an app OIDC and SAML browser sign-in ✅ Sign-in only; never a v3 API credential OAuth 2.0 and OIDC provider ✅ Scoped tokens for third-party applications, confinable to chosen libraries and collections; requires a stable public URL Passkeys and optional second factors ✅ Passkeys require a stable public URL Import a personal library from zotero.org ✅ Preserves object keys and versions Zotero iOS and Android apps ⚠️ Unofficial: needs a build pointed at altero; Android reported working on a device, iOS untested

items.title: Synchronization and API behavior implemented
items.text:
altero implements the parts of the v3 API needed by the desktop client, including:

  • API-key authentication and per-library permissions;
  • OAuth 2.0 access tokens as a second credential for the same endpoints;
  • personal and group library discovery;
  • item, collection, saved-search and tag reads;
  • json, atom, keys and versions response formats;
  • pagination, sorting, since and version-aware conditional requests;
  • item, collection and saved-search writes with version preconditions;
  • deleted-object synchronization;
  • library settings;
  • attachment full text;
  • the three-step attachment file protocol;
  • the streaming API at /stream;
  • My Publications and publication visibility;
  • citations, bibliographies, CSL JSON and Zotero export formats;
  • group creation, membership and group policy;
  • rate limiting when enabled; and
  • API version negotiation.

The compatibility reference documents behavior that differs from the public API documentation or that had to be learned from the real client or server: Compatibility notes.

Three explicit choices: library tag counts include trash, group renames notify clients, and Unfiled is a browser-only view.

items.title: Additional altero features
items.text: The browser adds account management, collection-sharing links, group activity, per-member restrictions, configurable retention and storage reporting. Library archives and migration from zotero.org support moving data between servers. See the web guide and administration guide.

items.title: Sign-in and authorization verification
items.text:
Live integration tests cover Keycloak and SimpleSAMLphp sign-in, and Authlib as a client of altero's authorization server. Other provider recipes are explicitly marked unverified in Administration.

The recorded OpenID Foundation assessment passed Config OP but did not pass Basic OP. altero is not OpenID-certified; see results and limits.

items.title: Not implemented
items.text:
• Storage quotas: usage is reported, but no per-library quota is enforced.
  • Continuous replication with zotero.org in either direction. The existing personal-library import is a one-time copy; one-way refresh remains future work.
  • Zotero's Note HTML and Note Markdown translators. These create a note rather than an ordinary bibliography/export response.
  • Zotero-hosted read-aloud speech synthesis and credit services (/tts/...).
  • Legacy password-to-key creation (POST /keys); use desktop browser linking or an API key.
  • Legacy removestoragefiles; synced attachment removal follows item deletion.

items.title: Client requests without a reference server implementation
items.text:
Two client behaviors do not have a corresponding implementation in the public dataserver source:

  • GET /retractions/list; and
  • the streaming WebSocket service.

altero currently answers the retractions request with 404. Zotero logs the failure and continues syncing. The streaming API is implemented from the published protocol and observed client behavior.

items.title: Library versions and concurrent writes
items.text:
Writes to a library are serialized so one request advances the library by one version, even when that request changes several objects. This is important because Zotero synchronization uses the library version as its consistency boundary.

See Database schema for the implementation details.

items.title: Checking a rootless Podman deployment
items.text:
Use this procedure to report a rootless run in issue #52. It exercises SQLite, the web interface, attachment storage, container replacement and the image's health check. See the historical run for one tested configuration. PostgreSQL, Compose and systemd integration need separate reports.

Use a Linux account with rootless Podman already configured, a browser and curl. Run the following blocks in the same shell, stopping on any failure. Use a new container and volume name for each attempt so a failed run's data remains available for inspection.

items.title: Record the host and image
items.text:
podman version
podman info --format '{{.Host.Security.Rootless}}'
podman info --format '{{.Store.GraphDriverName}}'

altero_probe_image=ghcr.io/eseifert/altero:latest
altero_probe_name=altero-rootless-check
altero_probe_volume=altero-rootless-check-data
altero_probe_port=18080
altero_probe_url="http://127.0.0.1:${altero_probe_port}"

podman pull "$altero_probe_image"
podman image inspect --format '{{.Id}} {{.Digest}} {{.Config.User}}' "$altero_probe_image"

Choose the image tag you want to test; latest includes prereleases. Record its resolved digest. The rootless field must be true. Run these commands as the ordinary account that will own the containers. Podman info also records the host, storage driver and namespace mappings if setup fails. Record the image ID and digest: a report about another image does not establish that a newer build works. For a source build, use the Docker image format and record its commit and image ID.

items.title: Start with a new volume
items.text:
podman volume create "$altero_probe_volume"
podman run --detach --name "$altero_probe_name" \
  --publish "127.0.0.1:${altero_probe_port}:8000" \
  --volume "${altero_probe_volume}:/data" \
  "$altero_probe_image"

curl --fail --retry 60 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 --retry-max-time 180 \
  --max-time 5 "$altero_probe_url/health"
curl --fail --output /dev/null "$altero_probe_url/app/"
podman exec "$altero_probe_name" id -u
podman healthcheck run "$altero_probe_name"

The readiness request retries for up to three minutes, including connection resets while migrations and server startup finish. The process UID must be 10001, and the health check must exit with code 0. A fresh named volume lets Podman initialise the mount's ownership for the image user; see volume ownership. If the check fails, preserve podman logs and inspect the health-check state using Podman's health-check commands.

Create a disposable account and set its password interactively:

podman exec -it "$altero_probe_name" altero user add podmancheck
podman exec -it "$altero_probe_name" altero user password podmancheck

Open http://127.0.0.1:18080/app/ (using your selected host port) and sign in. In the web library, create a book, add a note with recognisable text and attach a small local file. Download the attachment and compare its SHA-256 with the original. Keep the original file and the expected digest for the next step. Successful attachment upload checks that the application's mapped user can write the storage directory.

items.title: Replace the container and change its internal port
items.text:
Keep the volume while removing only the disposable container. Start its replacement with the same image and volume but internal port 8091:

podman stop "$altero_probe_name"
podman rm "$altero_probe_name"
podman run --detach --name "$altero_probe_name" \
  --env ALTERO_PORT=8091 \
  --publish "127.0.0.1:${altero_probe_port}:8091" \
  --volume "${altero_probe_volume}:/data" \
  "$altero_probe_image"

curl --fail --retry 60 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 --retry-max-time 180 \
  --max-time 5 "$altero_probe_url/health"
podman healthcheck run "$altero_probe_name"
podman exec "$altero_probe_name" id -u

The health check must again succeed, and the UID must still be 10001. Sign in again, check that the book and note survived, and download the same attachment. Its digest must still match the original. This checks persistence across container replacement as well as the health check's configured port.

items.title: Report the result
items.text:
Include the date, distribution and kernel, Podman version, rootless result, storage driver, image ID/digest, and whether each step passed. Say that this was a named-volume SQLite run. Report bind mounts, PostgreSQL, Compose or Quadlet separately, with their configuration differences.

Keep failed runs and their logs for diagnosis. Remove passwords, API keys, cookies and storage tokens before sharing logs. After a successful report, the disposable container and volume can be removed explicitly:

podman stop "$altero_probe_name"
podman rm "$altero_probe_name"
podman volume rm "$altero_probe_volume"
